records.title: APEX: A Dual-Sparsity Accelerator for Precise and Efficient SNN Inference
records.authors: D. B. Venkatesh, S. Radhakrishnan, R. Rakshit, G. Srinivasan
records.content:
# APEX: A Dual-Sparsity Accelerator for Precise and Efficient SNN Inference

**Authors.** D. B. Venkatesh, S. Radhakrishnan, R. Rakshit, G. Srinivasan  
**Venue.** arXiv 2608.19046  
**Date.** 2026-08-19  
**Links.**
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19046

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Integrates PASCAL's PASC-IF neuron into the LoAS fully temporal-parallel accelerator as a combinational three-stage datapath. Restates PASC-IF's stage durations as L_{n-1} timesteps (excitatory accumulation), max(L_{n-1}, L_n) - 1 (inhibitory correction) and L_n (output generation), so a PASC-IF layer's serial latency is L_{n-1} + max(L_{n-1}, L_n) - 1 + L_n rather than L_n. APEX avoids that serial cost only because the dataflow resolves the full post-synaptic tensor before the neuron unit runs, so the T-step spike train arrives as a bit vector and the stages collapse into three clock cycles; the output is regenerated as a bit vector for the next layer. Evaluated at uniform T (T4, T8) with mixed-precision weights only. Reports power, area, energy.

## Why it matters for the thesis

Cites PASCAL; first deployment study of PASCAL's neuron. Gives a concrete per-layer serial latency for PASC-IF that makes the average-T figure unattainable under sequential execution even before block boundaries. Does not implement per-layer T.

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution
- Bears on: Contribution 2 (QCFS++, block-wise execution and the deployability gap)

Logged in [[01-Literature/2026-09-14-literature-update|the 2026-09-14 literature update]].

Maps each `ANN2SNN_*`/`ANN_SNN_*`-style code folder in the repo root to the paper it implements. Paper filenames were renamed to drop the `ANN2SNN_`/`ANN_SNN_` prefix — just the method name — so the two sides read the same at a glance.

| Repo folder | Method | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| `ANN_SNN_QCFS` | QCFS | [[01-Literature/03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/02-Low-Latency/01-Activation-Level/QCFS.pdf\|QCFS]] |
| `ANN2SNN_COS` | COS | [[01-Literature/03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/02-Low-Latency/02-Neuron-Model-Level/COS.pdf\|COS]] |
| `ANN2SNN_GN` | GN | [[01-Literature/03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/02-Low-Latency/02-Neuron-Model-Level/GN.pdf\|GN]] |

| `ANN2SNN_QAC` | QAC | [[01-Literature/03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/03-Quant-Dist-Aware/01-Activation-Level/01-QAC/QAC.pdf\|QAC]] |

- Repo folders live at the Thesis repo root (outside the vault), e.g. `/Thesis/ANN2SNN_COS/`.

- If more `ANN2SNN_*`/`ANN_SNN_*` code folders get added later, add a row here and rename the corresponding paper to match (strip the prefix, keep the method name).

records.title: Literature
records.content:
# Literature

Papers only — one note per paper eventually goes in `01-Literature/notes/` (own-words summary + key takeaways, not a copy of the abstract). PDFs live in the numbered topic folders below, on disk, kept out of git via `.gitignore`. Every level of the tree is numbered for sort order, not just the top-level groups — subfolders and their children all carry a `NN-` prefix reflecting the order the topic is introduced in the thesis narrative (general/foundational first, surveys/supplementary material last).

This structure mirrors the actual sectioning of the thesis proposal's Background and Literature Review chapter (`04-Writing/Thesis_Proposal/main.tex`) — Quantization → SNN Fundamentals → ANN-to-SNN Conversion → Hardware, in that order — rather than an ad-hoc topic grouping. Auxiliary buckets (Tools, Surveys, Theses, NAS, Dr. Mohamed's list, Optimization, Courses, Exploratory) follow after the four core sections.

## Structure

- `00-Unsorted/` — 9 papers dropped at Literature root during the move-in, still needs manual triage
- `01-Quantization/` — 63 papers.
  - `01-Fundamentals/`: `01-Basics/` (general quantization methods) → `02-Uniform-Quantization/` → `03-Non-Uniform/` → `04-Clipping-Related/` (PTQ/calibration) → `05-Custom-STE/` (QAT) → `06-QAT-LSQ/` → `07-Mixed-Precision/` (with nested `01-New/`) → `08-Inference-Time-Decoding/` → `09-Surveys/` (the 3 true quantization surveys pulled out of the old Surveys folder)
  - `02-Distribution-Shaping/`: `01-Uniformization/` (`01-KURE/`, `02-Uniform-Distribution/`, plus EQ-Net/KurTail/SqWQ/GDRQ loose) → `02-Reshaping/` (`01-Bin-Regularization/` → `02-BR-Extension-Papers/` → `03-Activation-Distribution/` → `04-Wasserstein-EMD-Loss/` → `05-Sinusoidal-Regularization/` → `06-From-Dara/`) → `03-Outlier-Bias-Redistribution/` (empty placeholder)
- `02-SNN-Fundamentals/` — 6 papers. `01-Surveys/` (general SNN survey papers reclaimed from the old Surveys folder) — a placeholder to grow `02-Neuron-Models/`, `03-Spike-Encoding/`, `04-Training-SNNs/` into as specific papers get added
- `03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/` — 44 papers, ordered to match the thesis exactly:
  - `01-Classical-Conversion/`: `01-Foundational-Papers/` → `02-Unevenness-Error/` (with nested `01-BPTT/`) → `03-Membrane-Potential/`
  - `02-Low-Latency/`: `01-Activation-Level/` (QCFS lineage, SlipReLU) → `02-Neuron-Model-Level/` (signed/bipolar neurons, SignGD, SFN, SpikePack, LAS) → `03-Encoding-Level/` (Adaptive Fission, DCGS, phase/temporal coding)
  - `03-Quant-Dist-Aware/`: `01-Activation-Level/` (with nested `01-QAC/`, `02-MPQ/` — PASCAL) → `02-Neuron-Model-Encoding-Level/` (Fast-SNN, NeuBridge)
  - Paper filenames in this section (`QCFS.pdf`, `COS.pdf`, `GN.pdf`, `SRP.pdf`, `PASCAL.pdf`, `Fast-SNN.pdf`, `SNN_meets_ANN.pdf`) were renamed to match the repo's `ANN2SNN_*`/`ANN_SNN_*` code-folder naming — see [[01-Literature/03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/00-code-paper-lookup|Code ↔ Paper Lookup]] for the full code-to-paper mapping.
- `04-Hardware/` — 45 papers. `01-Embedded-Platforms/` (`01-MAX78000/` with nested `01-Papers/`) → `02-Neuromorphic-Platforms/` (`01-BrainChip-Akida/`, Loihi deployments) → `03-Surveys/` (the 9 TinyML/embedded-hardware surveys that were mislabeled as "Quantization-Surveys")
- `05-Neuromorphic-Background/` — 7 papers. `01-Intro/` → `02-Neuromorphic-Vision/` → `03-General-Surveys/` (2 high-level neuromorphic-computing reviews reclaimed from Surveys)
- `06-Neuromorphic-Applications/` — 6 papers. `01-Event-Based-Sensing/` + loose applied papers (fall detection, eye tracking, object detection) — kept as its own group alongside Background, not folded into the four core sections
- `07-Tools/` — 12 papers + 1 note. `01-Papers-on-SNNToolBox/` → `02-SpikingJelly/` — kept as its own group rather than distributed into Conversion/Hardware
- `08-Surveys/` — empty. Its contents got redistributed into the sections above once we realized most of it was mislabeled (TinyML/embedded surveys, not quantization surveys); kept as an empty placeholder for future non-fitting survey papers
- `09-Theses/` — 8 papers. `01-Neuromorphic/` → `02-Samples/` (labmate precedent work) + loose root theses
- `10-NAS/` — 3 papers, unchanged. Neural architecture search for SNNs (no subfolders to number)
- `11-Dr-Mohamed/` — 11 papers, unchanged numbering. Advisor's reading list — mostly State Space Models (SSMs) applied to SNNs/neuromorphic computing, plus the "Constrained Optimization Reformulation of Bin Regularization" proposal (moved here from Exploratory)
- `12-Optimization/` — 6 papers, unchanged. Multi-objective/Pareto optimization research papers (no subfolders to number)
- `13-Optimization-Background/` — 6 papers, unchanged. Convex-optimization foundations/textbook, primal-dual formulation, lecture notes (no subfolders to number)
- `14-Courses/` — lecture slide decks (`01-Neuromorphic Computing Course/`, 10 modules), not papers, not your own writing. Moved here from the vault root since it's reference/background material — kept as its own group rather than folded into a paper-based section
- `15-Exploratory/` — 2 papers. Loss-landscape/mode-connectivity papers not yet folded into a track (no subfolders to number)

## Index

- [[01-Literature/_index/00-unsorted|Unsorted]]
- [[01-Literature/_index/01-quantization|Quantization]]
- [[01-Literature/_index/02-snn-fundamentals|SNN Fundamentals]]

- [[01-Literature/_index/12-optimization|Optimization]]

- [[01-Literature/14-Courses/00-courses-MOC|Courses]]

Each link opens a small index note for that folder, which links to its own papers and, if it has subfolders, to their index notes in turn — real branching structure in Graph view instead of one flat starburst. (`08-Surveys` has no index note since it's currently empty; `14-Courses` links to its own hub note instead of an auto-generated index.)

## Updates

- A few placements were judgment calls made from titles/abstracts rather than full reads — worth a second look eventually: the loose `01-Quantization/02-Distribution-Shaping/` root file (general distribution theory, not clearly Uniformization or Reshaping), and a couple of general Low-Latency-Conversion papers filed at that level rather than in a specific Activation/Neuron/Encoding subfolder.
- Known duplicate PDF: `Improving_Low-Precision_Network_Quantization_via_Bin_Regularization.pdf` still exists as two copies in `01-Quantization/02-Distribution-Shaping/02-Reshaping/01-Bin-Regularization/` (one suffixed `(dup)`) — not yet deduplicated.
- `.gitignore` entry to keep Literature PDFs out of git — recommended early, still worth double-checking it's actually in place.

## 1. Orientation

### 1.1 How to read this report

The thesis retains the established term **ANN-to-SNN conversion**, while its empirical and deployment work focuses on **convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with ReLU-based activations**. Transformer conversion papers in this report provide related evidence on quantization, temporal precision, and execution. Transformer architectures are outside the thesis's experimental scope.

The opening table records the current status of the three focal papers. The next four sections contain the complete evidence for the 2026 landscape, mixed-timestep publication lineage, deployability, and Contributions 1 and 3. Each section ends with the consequence for the thesis. The companion [[2026-09-14-literature-refresh-positioning|positioning memo]] converts those consequences into edits, while [[2026-09-14-literature-update]] indexes the paper notes created during the refresh.

Each paper has one **canonical home** in the research family where its full profile belongs. Later analytical sections use short cross-references instead of hiding a second partial profile elsewhere. Evidence-depth labels have the following meanings:

- **Full text checked** — the paper or proceedings PDF was inspected beyond its abstract.
- **Publisher record and abstract checked** — authoritative metadata and abstract or publisher highlights were available, but the full paper was not inspected.
- **Abstract/index record only** — the accessible evidence was an abstract or bibliographic index; detailed claims and exact results remain unverified.
- **Status unresolved** — no authoritative final decision or publication record is currently available.

| Work | Current record | Central finding for the thesis |
|---|---|---|
| **PASCAL** — Ramesh and Srinivasan | TMLR, published 10 December 2025; arXiv:2505.01730 v2 | Its reported `T_eff` is an energy-ratio-weighted mean, not latency. The only wall-clock test uses uniform `T=4`. Cite the TMLR version and its revised 56× headline. |
| **QAC** — Guo et al. | Rejected ICLR 2025 submission; no archival successor found | It is the closest mixed-timestep/QAT precursor and states the approximate forward equivalence, but supplies neither deployment nor the QCFS backward-pass identity. |
| **MT-SNN** — Guo et al. | Withdrawn ICLR 2026 submission; accepted by *Frontiers in Neuroscience* on 12 August 2026 | It still reports the unweighted mean `T̄=Σ_lT_l/L`; SSCA aligns in the synaptic-current domain. It has GPU timing but no neuromorphic execution. |

The consolidated verdicts are:

1. **Contribution 1 is narrowed, not lost.** Fast-SNN, QAC, SpikeZIP-TF, Li–Ma–Furber, and others anticipate the forward QAT-to-SNN relationship. The remaining claim is the exact two-directional QCFS identity, including `T=2^b-1`, scale and rounding conventions, the learnable-threshold gradient, and an independent bit-identical witness.
2. **Contribution 2 remains open with better-defined prior art.** Five current methods use non-uniform horizons or budgets, but all report a mean or average proxy. Block grouping and boundary transformations have precedents; the unoccupied part is external assignment, a costed boundary-operator taxonomy, dual sequential/pipelined accounting, and an actual SpikingJelly/Lava/Loihi execution path.
3. **Contribution 3 should be decoder-centred.** Constant-threshold count decoding produces a uniform grid; linear-kernel TTFS can also be uniform; geometric weighting, time-varying thresholds, and graded payloads induce other families. The defensible contribution is a decoder-to-quantizer-family taxonomy, not the blanket claim that temporal coding is logarithmic quantisation.
4. **The implementation baseline has changed.** SpikingJelly 2.0 already provides `SpikeCountToBinary` and `TemporalBinSum`. They are useful substrates for count/re-encode boundaries, but they do not provide heterogeneous per-layer horizons.

### 1.2 Research-family locator

This locator is the shortest route to each paper's full method context. Contribution sections may cite the same paper to answer a narrower question, but the family section is where the reader should begin.

Focal papers, citations, and mixed-timestep successors]]                                                                                | Publication histories; cited-by evidence; corrected MT-SNN record                                                                                            |

---

## 2. Broad 2026 landscape, allocator inputs, and surveys

### 2.1 Low-latency ANN-to-SNN conversion landscape

#### 2.1.1 QCFS family and direct extensions

This is the canonical home for papers that explicitly start from QCFS, modify its activation or conversion dynamics, or evaluate an extension directly on QCFS models. PASCAL therefore belongs here as a direct QCFS-family method as well as in the focal-paper and mixed-timestep analysis in [[#3.1.1 PASCAL: Ramesh and Srinivasan, IIT Madras]]. Their relevance to the backward-pass/QAT claim is analysed later in [[#5.1 Papers framing conversion or QCFS as QAT or fake quantisation]]; that separate question should not determine whether a paper is visible in the QCFS family itself.

| Work | Venue / year | Relationship to QCFS | Main modification | Granularity | Representative low-`T` result | Evidence depth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[#5.1.3 Passing remarks\|QCFS]] | ICLR 2022 | Family root and reference activation | Clip–floor–shift activation trained with an STE, then mapped to a soft-reset IF neuron | One learned threshold `λ` per layer | Baseline against which the extensions below report their gains | Full text checked |
| [[#3.1.1 PASCAL: Ramesh and Srinivasan, IIT Madras\|PASCAL]] | TMLR 2025 | Direct QCFS-based conversion method; Theorem 3.6 proves equivalence between its PASC-SNN formulation and the QCFS ANN | Spike accumulation with PASC-IF plus adaptive layer-wise activation horizons | Layer | `T_eff=3.14` for the reported ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 assignment; this is an energy-weighted mean, not latency | Full TMLR text, appendix, and code record checked |
| [[#2.1.1.1 CS-QCFS: channel-wise positive thresholds\|CS-QCFS]] | *Neural Networks*, 2025 | Direct QCFS activation extension | Channel-wise Softplus thresholds prevent negative thresholds and model channel heterogeneity | Channel | CIFAR-10 95.86%; CIFAR-100 74.83%, both at `T=1` | Publisher record and abstract checked |
| [[#2.1.1.2 Residual membrane-potential alignment\|Residual membrane-potential alignment]] | arXiv, August 2026 | Trains and refines a QCFS model | Residual-potential regularisation plus `SCR-Conv2d` refinement | Initial potential and channel group | CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 93.65% at `T=2`; QCFS re-run 92.86% | Full text checked |
| [[#2.1.1.3 Error Compensation Learning\|Error Compensation Learning]] | ICML 2025 | Adds a conversion mechanism to QCFS | Learned error compensation with dual-threshold neurons | Neuron / threshold mechanism | CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 94.75% at `T=2`; ImageNet VGG-16 74.15% at `T=16` | Full text and proceedings record checked |
| [[#2.1.1.4 Group-wise threshold distribution and codebook alignment\|Group-wise threshold and codebook alignment]] | IEEE DLCV 2026 | Direct QCFS-based enhancement | Group-wise clipping/scale learning plus codebook-state alignment | Channel group | Improvement reported on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet; exact values inaccessible | Abstract/index record only |
| [[#2.1.2.1 Adaptive Fission\|Adaptive Fission]] | NeurIPS 2025 | QCFS-compatible, but not QCFS-exclusive | Post-training splitting of sensitive neurons trades spatial/population memory for shorter horizons | Neuron | QCFS/ResNet-20/CIFAR-100 72.15% at `T=4`, versus 55.25% without fission | Full text and Table 1 checked |

##### 2.1.1.1 CS-QCFS: channel-wise positive thresholds

**CS-QCFS: Bridging the Performance Gap in Ultra-Low Latency Spiking Neural Networks.** Hongchao Yang, Suorong Yang, Lingming Zhang, Hui Dou, Furao Shen, Jian Zhao. *Neural Networks* 184:107076, 2025. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2024.107076

**Evidence depth: publisher record and abstract checked.** CS-QCFS means **Channel-wise Softplus QCFS**. It identifies channel-wise activation heterogeneity and the possibility of invalid negative learned thresholds in a single layer-wide QCFS parameterisation. It therefore learns clipping thresholds per channel and passes them through Softplus so that the resulting thresholds remain positive. This is a direct QCFS-family method, not merely an adjacent 2025 quantisation paper.

The publisher material reports the following ultra-low-latency results at `T=1`:

| Dataset | Reported top-1 accuracy at `T=1` |
|---|---:|
| CIFAR-10 | 95.86% |
| CIFAR-100 | 74.83% |

**Relevance.** CS-QCFS strengthens the evidence that channel-wise threshold or scale learning is established inside the QCFS lineage. It does not, in the accessible material, prove a QCFS-to-standard-QAT backward identity, compare the QCFS threshold gradient with LSQ or PACT, or provide an independent bit-identical witness. Those are distinct Contribution 1 questions.

##### 2.1.1.2 Residual membrane-potential alignment

**Reducing ANN-SNN Conversion Error via Residual Membrane Potential Alignment.** Zirui Chen, Zihan Huang, Tong Bu, Jianhao Ding, Yiting Dong, Zhaofei Yu (Peking University). arXiv:2608.13952, 14 August 2026, no venue stated. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13952

**Evidence depth: full text checked.** The method attributes unevenness and quantization error at small `T` to the residual membrane-potential distribution. It adds a regularizer `L_RMPD` on a trainable initial potential, initialized at the QCFS value `0.5`, plus a grouped-convolution `SCR-Conv2d` refinement layer. It is applied on top of QCFS and compared with QCFS, SRP, and SNM. Table I below preserves the reported values; the parenthesised QCFS numbers are the authors' re-runs.

| Dataset / architecture | ANN | T = 2 | T = 4 | T = 8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 | 96.57 | 93.65 (QCFS 92.86) | 95.50 (94.92) | 96.33 (96.21) |
| CIFAR-10 VGG-16 | 95.65 | 92.84 (90.67) | 94.80 (94.21) | 95.66 (95.40) |
| CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 | 91.84 | 78.41 (77.74) | 86.95 (86.52) | 91.04 (90.79) |
| CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 | 78.46 | 69.73 (69.36) | 76.05 (75.45) | 78.48 (78.55) |
| CIFAR-100 VGG-16 | 76.45 | 65.72 (64.95) | 72.69 (71.24) | 76.96 (75.14) |
| CIFAR-100 ResNet-20 | 64.74 | 38.52 (36.16) | 53.25 (50.75) | 62.82 (61.56) |
ImageNet only from T=16 (VGG-16 56.46 vs QCFS 50.92; ResNet-34 60.74 vs 60.52). No T=1. No code URL found. The QCFS authors' own group still calls QCFS "the state-of-the-art baseline" in August 2026.

##### 2.1.1.3 Error Compensation Learning

**Efficient ANN-SNN Conversion with Error Compensation Learning.** Chang Liu et al. ICML 2025. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/liu25bl.html

**Evidence depth: full text/proceedings record checked.** This method uses dual-threshold neurons on top of QCFS and learns to compensate conversion error. It reports ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 at 94.75% for `T=2` and 95.99% for `T=4`, and VGG-16 on ImageNet at 74.15% for `T=16`. It is the principal dual-threshold reference point in this report. Its neuron widens the state/output mechanism relative to binary single-threshold QCFS; this distinction matters when comparing apparent timestep reductions.

##### 2.1.1.4 Group-wise threshold distribution and codebook alignment

**Group-Wise Threshold Distribution Learning and Codebook State Alignment for Low-Timestep ANN-SNN Conversion.** X. Ji, H. Zhao, Y. Chen. IEEE DLCV 2026. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1109/DLCV69906.2026.11635228

**Evidence depth: abstract/index record only.** The abstract describes this explicitly as a lightweight enhancement for QCFS-based conversion. Group-Wise Threshold Distribution Learning (GTDL) assigns channel-group clipping ranges and quantisation scales, while codebook-bridge regularisation aligns quantised ANN activations with the target low-timestep spiking states. It reports evaluation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with improved conversion accuracy; exact results and the expanded author names remain unavailable. This paper belongs here because it is a direct QCFS follow-up even though only abstract-level evidence is available.

#### 2.1.2 QCFS-compatible post-training precision extensions

##### 2.1.2.1 Adaptive Fission

**Adaptive Fission: Post-training Encoding for Low-latency Spike Neural Networks.** Yizhou Jiang et al. NeurIPS 2025. Abstract: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/e2e0a9004132490db1be58bffa419268-Abstract-Conference.html. Paper: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/e2e0a9004132490db1be58bffa419268-Paper-Conference.pdf

**Evidence depth: full text checked, including Table 1.** Adaptive Fission is a post-training population/precision allocation method rather than a new QCFS activation. It identifies sensitive neurons and splits them so that a lower temporal horizon can retain more representational states. The method is evaluated on Calib, QCFS, SRP, STA, TEBN, and a spike-driven transformer, so QCFS is one supported base rather than the method's only lineage.

The previously reported “1.6× memory for an 8× timestep reduction” is one configuration, not a universal or accuracy-preserving trade. For Calib/ResNet-20/CIFAR-100, the baseline at `T=32` is 76.32%, 0.85 GB, 56.8 s per epoch, and 0.64 Wh. Fission at `T=4` is 73.11%, 1.31 GB, 12.0 s, and 0.18 Wh: 8× fewer timesteps, 1.54× memory, 4.73× faster epochs, 71.9% less energy, and a 3.21-point accuracy loss.

The complete Table 1 transcription follows so the configuration dependence is visible rather than buried in a single ratio.



**Relevance.** Adaptive Fission is a strong precedent for trading temporal precision against spatial/population memory, but it does not assign one deployable `T_l` per layer or provide the block-boundary and dual-schedule model proposed in Contribution 2.

#### 2.1.3 Single-timestep conversion via multi-valued or multi-threshold spikes

| Work | Status | Mechanism | Representative result | Interpretation for the thesis | Source |

### 2.5 Broad-landscape consequences for the thesis

Must be added to Background: (1) Chen et al. arXiv:2608.13952 as the current QCFS-family state of the art at T=2,4,8; (2) PMSM and Scale-and-Fire as the T=1 results, with an explicit statement of the thesis's spike model (binary, one spike per neuron per step, reset by subtraction) because both rely on multi-valued or multi-threshold spikes; (3) closed-loop CKA distillation (ICML 2026) as post-conversion fine-tuning; (4) AAAI-26 training-free conversions and Adaptive Fission as the no-retraining branch; (5) InfoQ as the concrete allocator emitting per-layer activation scores, MetaMix as the activation-only precedent, PTQ4SNN as the SNN-internal analogue; (6) NeuroTrain, the NCE acceleration survey, and Kranzlmüller et al. for positioning and energy claims.

Positioning: uniform-T QCFS is not obsolete at T=2 or T=4 on CNNs; the QCFS group's own August 2026 paper adds one to two points and reports no T=1. At T=1 the shift comes only from widening the per-step channel, so a multi-threshold neuron with K thresholds and a block with T_b steps are two ways to spend the same precision budget, and both need a deployable execution model; this turns the T=1 papers into a motivation for Contribution 2 rather than a threat. QAC's Theorem 1 and PMSM anticipate the forward relationship only; [[#5. Contribution 1: QCFS as activation-only QAT|Section 5]] gives the precise novelty boundary.

**Unresolved records:** the acceptance status of Scale-and-Fire, the abstract and quantitative results of Xia et al. (*Neurocomputing* 2026), and an official MetaMix implementation. Adaptive Fission Table 1 and GMPQ-TE's activation/code scope are resolved above.

The central Contribution 2 result is visible in the fourth column: none of the verified PASCAL citations implements or evaluates its per-layer activation-horizon assignment. In this report, **mixed temporal precision** means that different layers receive different activation horizons (`T_l` varies with `l`); a **uniform activation horizon** means one shared value (`T_1=…=T_L=T`). The two PASCAL-citing hardware follow-ups, NeuroFlex and APEX, use the latter. APEX mixes INT4/INT8 **weights**, while NeuroFlex mixes ANN/SNN computation at column granularity; neither mixes activation precision through per-layer timesteps.

Citation tracing answers a deliberately narrow question—who has explicitly taken up PASCAL, QAC, or MT-SNN. The following subsection places those citation lineages alongside the full nearby literature: methods that independently use layer-, stage-, modality-, or block-level temporal heterogeneity, whether or not they cite one of the three focal papers.

#### 3.2.1 Detailed PASCAL citation records

Four PASCAL citations are verified:

1. **NeuroFlex: Column-Exact ANN-SNN Co-Execution Accelerator with Cost-Guided Scheduling.** V. Manjunath, P. Ramesh, G. Srinivasan. arXiv 2511.05215, 7 November 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05215. Extends PASCAL's integer-exact QCFS conversion from layers to individual output columns; stores all activations as INT8 and generates spikes on the fly inside the PE ("Spike Generation / Spike Count / Membrane Potential Reinitialization"), with `(3L−1)=23` timesteps for `L=8`; an offline cost model assigns columns to ANN or SNN cores with "deterministic runtime". States that "the effective number of timesteps remains the same as that specified in (Ramesh & Srinivasan, 2025)". Cost: throughput and EDP from an accelerator model. Uniform `T`.

2. **APEX: A Dual-Sparsity Accelerator for Precise and Efficient SNN Inference.** D. B. Venkatesh, S. Radhakrishnan, R. Rakshit, G. Srinivasan. arXiv 2608.19046, 19 August 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19046. Implements the PASC-IF neuron as a combinational three-stage datapath inside LoAS; fully temporal-parallel dataflow processes all `T` in parallel. "Mixed precision" refers to INT4/INT8 weights chosen per layer; activations run at uniform `T`. Reports power, area, and energy, but no per-layer timesteps.

3. **Analysis of the Relation Between Bitdepth and Timesteps in ANN to SNN Conversion.** C. Steennis. MSc thesis, LIACS, Leiden University, 29 August 2025; supervisors J. Broekens and Q. Chen. [Landing page](https://theses.liacs.nl/3527); [PDF](https://theses.liacs.nl/pdf/2024-2025-SteennisCChristian.pdf). Empirically concludes that "the known bound `T=2^b−1` is a huge overestimation" and fits a logistic relation between bit depth and required `T`. The work is indexed as citing PASCAL, although the in-text use is not visible in the available excerpts, which cite Bu et al. and Datta et al.

4. **SNN-IDS: Deploying SNN-Equivalent Intrusion Detection on a Commodity MCU NPU.** H.-C. Tsai. Preprints.org 202603.0817, revised version 2. https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202603.0817.v2. Cites PASCAL as reference 13 in passing ("refined multi-timestep conversion with spike accumulation and adaptive layerwise calibration") alongside NeuroFlex and NEXUS. Its own contribution is a `T=1` INT8 MLP on an STM32N6 NPU and the observation that QCFS's Floor operator falls back to the CPU, adding 17.6% latency. It was not yet present in the principal citation index.

### 3.5 Mixed-timestep consequences for the thesis

All relevant literature and its execution evidence have now been presented. The following conclusions distinguish what prior work already supplies from what the thesis can still claim.

#### 3.5.1 The execution-model gap

The claim that mixed-timestep networks have no stated execution model still holds, with two qualifications.

**==Nobody has executed a mixed-timestep converted SNN on a neuromorphic chip or a standard SNN simulator**==, nor reported `Σ_l T_l` or a pipelined `max_l T_l` plus fill/drain cost. PASCAL's only hardware latency number is for uniform `T=4`; MT-SNN reports GPU wall-clock; ==PseudoSN, Adaptive Bit Allocation, and SpikeMLLM report averages or budgets.== The claim should be stated precisely as “no execution model with a stated cost under sequential or pipelined semantics”, because two papers now gesture at one: Adaptive Bit Allocation (App. A.9) asserts pipelined overlap via SpikeConverter's two-stage accumulate/emit design without measuring it, and SpikeMLLM explicitly reframes `T` as arithmetic cost under temporal parallelism (the same move APEX and LoAS make). The thesis should engage both directly: the first is an unmeasured claim the block-wise experiments can test; the second concedes that on temporal-parallel hardware the “timestep” is not a latency at all, which supports the thesis's argument that the reported averages are not latencies.

The unweighted-mean metric is now used in at least four independent papers (QAC, MT-SNN, PseudoSN, Adaptive Bit Allocation), and PASCAL's `T_eff` is an energy-weighted mean. The thesis's critique should distinguish these two definitions; the PASCAL figure of 3.14 is defensible as an energy proxy and indefensible as a latency, and the paper never claims otherwise in the TMLR text.

#### 3.5.2 Novelty boundary and defensible combined claim

| Proposed element | Prior-art status | Defensible thesis position |
|---|---|---|
| External MPQ assignment as input | Allocators already exist; using one is not a standalone novelty | Deliberately assignment-agnostic interface that isolates the execution problem |
| Block/stage grouping | Established by SSNN, MTT, BlocTrain, pipeline partitioning, and BrainScaleS-2 partitioning | Deployment granularity, **not** a novelty claim |
| Per-layer `T_l` | Established by LD-SNN, PASCAL, QAC, MT-SNN, PseudoSNN, and Adaptive Bit Allocation | Assignment source and software upper bound, **not** a novelty claim |
| Blockification of a fixed MPQ QCFS assignment | No matching execution study found | Define the mapping from `L_l` to blocks and `T_b`, retrain at block precision, and measure retained accuracy |
| `B_count` / `B_reencode` / `B_align` | Individual operations have precedents | Claim the typed taxonomy, representation contract, and use as explicit block interfaces—not invention of the primitives |
| Sequential and pipelined reporting | Both cost models have systems precedents | Apply both to the same converted mixed-precision SNN with fill, drain, stall, buffering, and boundary terms |
| Fewer non-standard conversions | Per-layer methods can require an alignment at every changed boundary | Quantify the trade from up to `N−1` special interfaces to `K−1` block interfaces |
| SpikingJelly → Lava → Loihi validation | No verified mixed-`T` converted-SNN deployment found | Claim only after implementation and measurement |

**Defensible combined claim.** Given an externally supplied activation-MPQ assignment, QCFS++ converts it into a fixed block-level QCFS model and executes the converted SNN as timestep-homogeneous blocks connected by explicit, typed, and costed temporal boundaries. Its evaluation reports both sequential latency and realizable pipelined throughput, including fill, drain, stall, buffering, and boundary work. ==This complete bundle—not block grouping, per-layer `T`, or count/re-encode primitives separately—is where Contribution 2 sits.==

#### 3.5.3 Publication-status corrections

PASCAL should be cited as TMLR 2025, not only arXiv, with the 56× figure. QAC remains an unpublished ICLR 2025 submission with no verified citations; MT-SNN was withdrawn from ICLR 2026 and later accepted at *Frontiers in Neuroscience*, also with no verified citations. The reviewer-objection sentence about latency is not independently documented here; quote it only from a saved copy of the OpenReview forum.

#### 3.5.4 Incidental bearing on Contribution 1

Three papers in this set state the quantization-equals-timesteps identity: QAC (Theorem 1, `T ≡ 2^n` with soft reset), MT-SNN (the same theorem restated as an approximation), and PseudoSN (“equivalent to value quantization with T levels,” citing Bu et al. 2022 and Liu et al. 2025). None proves bit-identity of the QCFS training pass to a standard QAT quantizer with STE; QAC's theorem is a forward-pass rate-equivalence argument. This is consistent with the thesis's claim that the forward-and-backward identity and its bit-exact validation are unstated elsewhere, but the thesis must now cite QAC and PseudoSN as prior forward-pass statements.

#### 4.1.3 Hardware realisation of PASCAL's neuron

APEX (Venkatesh, Radhakrishnan, Rakshit, Srinivasan, arXiv 2608.19046, 19 Aug 2026) integrates PASCAL's PASC-IF neuron into the LoAS fully temporal-parallel (FTP) accelerator. Two facts matter for the thesis. First, the paper restates PASC-IF's stage durations as L_{n-1} timesteps (excitatory accumulation), max(L_{n-1}, L_n) - 1 timesteps (inhibitory correction), and L_n timesteps (output generation), so a PASC-IF layer's serial latency is not L_n but L_{n-1} + max(L_{n-1}, L_n) - 1 + L_n. Second, APEX sidesteps that serial cost only because the FTP dataflow "fully resolves the post-synaptic input tensor before the neuron unit is invoked", so the whole T-step spike train arrives as a bit vector and all three stages collapse into three combinational clock cycles; the output "C[1..L_n]" is regenerated as a bit vector for the next layer. Evaluated configurations are uniform T (T4, T8) with mixed-precision weights only. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19046. Classification (a): this is, in hardware, a count-then-regenerate boundary at every layer (LBL execution in ELSA's taxonomy), and it is the first deployment study of PASCAL. It does not implement PASCAL's per-layer T assignment and does not report latency under it.

### 4.3 Neuromorphic hardware and simulator support

#### 4.3.1 Loihi 2 and Lava

Global timestep in Lava. Runtime._run sends the same num_steps to every runtime service (for send_port in self.runtime_to_service: send_port.send(enum_to_np(self.num_steps))), and LoihiPyRuntimeService.run iterates the Loihi phases per timestep, broadcasting each phase to all ProcessModels in the sync domain and waiting for their DONE responses. https://github.com/lava-nc/lava/blob/main/src/lava/magma/runtime/runtime.py, https://github.com/lava-nc/lava/blob/main/src/lava/magma/runtime/runtime_services/runtime_service.py. The docs confirm that run() on any process "will also execute all Processes that are connected to it" for the given RunSteps(num_steps). https://lava-nc.org/lava/notebooks/in_depth/tutorial04_execution.html. There is no API to run one process for T = 4 and a connected process for T = 1 within one run call.
The only escape hatch is AsyncProtocol, under which "Processes are executed without synchronization on specific phases... could run with a varying speed". https://lava-nc.org/lava/lava.magma.core.sync.protocols.html. Mixing Loihi-protocol and async-protocol processes has documented deadlocks (issue #314, 2022), and the async protocol has no Loihi 2 neurocore backend. https://github.com/lava-nc/lava/issues/314.
On silicon the timestep is enforced by NoC barrier synchronization (Timcheck et al. 2026, above), and nxkernel exposes exactly two schedules, fall-through and pipelined (Brehove et al. 2026; Meyer et al. 2024, above). Per-layer horizons are not a configuration option in any of these sources.
Graded spikes. The Loihi 2 technology brief states that "Loihi 2 permits spikes to carry integer-valued payloads" and that neurons "can optionally generate and transmit graded spikes... that carry a 32-bit spike payload". https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/central-libraries/us/en/documents/neuromorphic-computing-loihi-2-brief.pdf. Brehove et al. use "up to 16 bit signed integer payloads" for quantized activations; an OSTI report on the Overflow neuron states each graded spike passes "a 32-bit integer value". https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/3004360. Intel's own ANN-style deployments on Loihi 2 (SDNN, S4D) therefore transmit multi-bit values once per timestep rather than counts over T steps. Consequence for the thesis: on Loihi 2, B_count is a native single-timestep message (one graded spike carrying the count), and B_reencode is the only boundary that costs T_b timesteps. No documented use applies graded spikes to per-layer activation mixed precision; the SDNN conversion uses a uniform 8-bit activation grid.
Lava provides no count-to-spike primitive beyond its sigma-delta and graded-spike neuron models.
#### 4.3.2 SpiNNaker 2

Timesteps are timer-tick driven per PE: "A timer tick triggers each time step and guarantees real time operation. In each time step, after the neurons are simulated, the output spikes are sent to their target PEs, where they are stored in a FIFO and processed in the next time step." https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.08392. The EventProp implementation runs a per-core systicks loop up to a shared n_timesteps with a global start interrupt (arXiv 2412.15021). SpiNNaker 2's DNN path (OctopuScheduler, arXiv 2507.13736) is strictly layer-by-layer under a scheduler PE, which is the sequential model. The documented py-spinnaker2 interface exposes no per-layer timestep control (https://spinnaker2.gitlab.io/py-spinnaker2/).

The newer primary chip manuscript, **“The SpiNNaker2 chip: a many-core platform for flexible and scalable brain-inspired computing,”** Stefan Scholze et al., arXiv:2607.24396, 27 July 2026, describes 152 processing elements, more than 150,000 neurons and 1.8 billion synaptic events/s at 1 ms, baseline power below 250 mW, and an INT8 DNN path reaching 4.5 TOPS or 2.7 TOPS/W. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24396. **Evidence depth: full primary hardware manuscript checked.** It strengthens the current hardware description but exposes no per-layer temporal-horizon control.

Krishna Kant Singh, Charl Linssen, Eric Müller, Eleni Mathioulaki, Wouter Klijn, Lena Oden, **“Unifying von-Neumann HPC and Neuromorphic Acceleration via the EBRAINS Research Infrastructure: A Framework for High-Performance Workflows,”** arXiv:2606.08515, 7 June 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08515. **Evidence depth: primary preprint record and abstract checked.** The workflow dispatches jobs to HPC and SpiNNaker1, with NESTML models usable through both NEST and sPyNNaker. It demonstrates model/job portability, not independent horizons inside one connected network.

#### 4.3.3 BrainScaleS-2

Continuous-time analog emulation ("the experiment in general cannot be paused"); deep networks are executed as sequential partitions with recorded and replayed events (Section 2, item 5). There is no discrete timestep to vary per layer, but the duration of each partition run is a free parameter of the experiment, which makes BSS-2 the one platform on which block-wise horizons are natively expressible.

#### 4.3.4 SynSense Speck and Xylo

Speck is fully asynchronous: "information communication with layers are only in 'event based' format, the layer process the 'incoming' event only at whenever a layer receives it"; a slow clock exists only for leak, DVS filtering, and readout averaging. https://github.com/synsense/sinabs/blob/develop/docs/speck/overview.md, https://sinabs.readthedocs.io/v3.1.2/speck/faqs/available_network_arch.html. There is no timestep to set per layer; rate-coded T is a property of the input presentation window, not of the chip.

#### 4.3.5 SpikingJelly

Checked the CHANGELOG for 2.0.0.dev1 (2026-08-14), 2.0.0.dev2 (2026-08-23), 2.0.0rc1 (2026-08-29), and Unreleased; grepped for per-layer, layerwise, heterogeneous, timestep. No feature adds per-layer T or heterogeneous multi-step horizons. Multi-step mode still passes a single [T, N, *] tensor layer to layer (seq_to_ann_forward, MultiStepContainer), so T is a global tensor dimension. The maintainer's own description of multi-step inference is "we give the SNN a constant input" repeated T times (issue #379). New but unrelated additions: ActivationAwareIFNode, SignedQCFSSequenceEncoder, NIR exchange, Lava and Lynxi exchange modules, and the count/bin layers in Section 2. https://github.com/fangwei123456/spikingjelly/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md, https://github.com/fangwei123456/spikingjelly/issues/379.

#### 4.3.6 Other adjacent 2026 hardware

Liyu Qian, Zikai Zhu, Yuhan He, Jie Lu, Yaojie Sun, Jiahui Guo, Lirong Zheng, Zhuo Zou, **“A compressed sensing neuromorphic processor for sparse signal classification,”** *Frontiers in Neuroscience* 20, 21 May 2026. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2026.1777090. **Evidence depth: full publisher article checked.** At compression ratios 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, and 0.01, the design reports at least 80% fewer operations. Its 40 nm estimate gives 96.12% MNIST accuracy with 8-bit data, 2.089 mW at 1.1 V and 100 MHz. The contribution is input/computation compression, not temporal-horizon scheduling.

The *Nature Electronics* SNN-in-logic architecture is profiled in [[#2.1.6 Other 2026 items: adjacent or background]]. It likewise reduces spatial work rather than assigning different `T_l` values.

None of the reviewed 2025–2026 schedulers assigns different temporal horizons to connected layers or blocks within one inference.

### 4.5 Deployability consequences for the thesis

#### 4.5.1 Does anything already provide the proposed execution model?

No. Five methods now produce per-layer T assignments—PASCAL, QAC, MT-SNN in *Frontiers* 2026, PseudoSNN in AAAI 2026, and Adaptive Bit Allocation—plus LD-SNN 2022 and SSNN 2024 as precursors; three of them define a boundary operator: SSNN's temporal transformer, PseudoSNN's temporal reshaping, and MT-SNN's SSCA. None states an execution model, and all report a mean of `T_l` as the latency or budget. The closest hardware precedents are APEX, with count-and-regenerate at every layer but uniform T only, and BrainScaleS-2 partitioned emulation, with sequential block execution and record-and-replay motivated by substrate size. The thesis's specific claims—that the boundary is a first-class operator with three variants and that cost must be reported under both sequential and pipelined schedules with fill, drain, stall, and boundary terms—remain unoccupied. Two items require immediate text changes: MT-SNN is now accepted (*Frontiers in Neuroscience*, August 2026), and SpikingJelly 2.0 ships `SpikeCountToBinary` and `TemporalBinSum`, which should be cited as the implementation substrate for `B_reencode` and `B_count` rather than presented as new.

#### 4.5.2 Is the “one global timestep” claim contradicted?

No, and it is now better supported than before, with one nuance. Loihi 2 synchronizes algorithmic timesteps by NoC barrier (Timcheck et al. 2026) and Lava's runtime broadcasts one `num_steps` to every process; SpiNNaker2 uses timer-tick timesteps per PE; SpikingJelly has no per-layer T. The nuance is BrainScaleS-2, which is continuous-time and executes deep networks as sequential hardware runs, so a per-block horizon is expressible there as the duration of each run. The thesis should say: “TrueNorth, Loihi, SpiNNaker, and SpikingJelly advance one global timestep; BrainScaleS-2 has no discrete timestep but executes partitions sequentially, which is the block-wise model by construction.” SynSense Speck should be listed as asynchronous with no timestep at all. Loihi 2's 32-bit graded spikes also change the count-versus-spike picture in the thesis's favour: `B_count` is a one-timestep message on Loihi 2, so only re-encoding costs `T_b` steps.

#### 4.5.3 Do the sources support the thesis's cost models?

Yes. The sequential model, a sum over blocks, corresponds to ELSA's LBL class, LD-SNN's measured layer-by-layer speedups, BSS-2 partition runs, and OctopuScheduler on SpiNNaker2. The pipelined model, a maximum over blocks plus fill and drain, corresponds to ELSA's TBT class, nxkernel's pipelined mode, and Meyer et al.'s fall-through-versus-pipelined continuum; Koopman et al. supply the argument that per-layer barriers set latency. The per-timestep constant multiplying both models is given by Intel's max-affine model with its explicit barrier term. APEX additionally supplies a concrete per-layer serial latency for PASC-IF, `L_{n-1} + max(L_{n-1}, L_n) - 1 + L_n`, which the thesis can use to show that PASCAL's own neuron makes the average-T figure unattainable under sequential execution even before block boundaries are considered.

#### 4.5.4 Explicit negative results

The reviewed literature contains no critique of average or effective timesteps in 2024–2026; no conversion paper with block-wise mixed-`T` execution and dual cost reporting; no Lava or Loihi 2 mechanism for per-process horizons; no SpikingJelly per-layer `T`; no 2025–2026 compiler or scheduler that assigns or executes distinct temporal horizons for connected layers or blocks; and no work on activation, as opposed to weight, mixed precision on Loihi 2. This does **not** mean that SNN schedulers are absent: MPL-schedule schedules heterogeneous whole tasks, and the configurable streaming accelerator balances per-layer spatial parallelism. Neither exposes `T_l` as a scheduling decision.

## 5. Contribution 1: QCFS as activation-only QAT

### 5.1 Papers framing conversion or QCFS as QAT or fake quantisation

The papers are ordered by strength of the statement.

#### 5.1.1 Formal statement with proof or explicit parameter mapping

Hu, Zheng, Jiang, Pan, "Fast-SNN: Fast Spiking Neural Network by Converting Quantized ANN", IEEE TPAMI 45(12), 2023 (arXiv May 2023). https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19868, https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2023.3275769
Section 3.1 (arXiv p. 4) defines a standard QAT quantizer, Eq. (1), Q = s/(2^b − 1) · clip(round((2^b − 1) x / s), 0, 2^b − 1), and the IF neuron with reset-by-subtraction, Eq. (6), r = (1/T) clip(floor(x̃/θ), 0, T), then states the mapping verbatim: "Comparing Eq. 6 with Eq. 1, we let μ^l = θ^l/2, T = 2^b − 1, θ^l = s^l. Since a flooring operator can be converted to a rounding operator floor(x + 0.5) = round(x), (8)". Section 3.2 (p. 5): "With Eq. 10, we then equivalently convert the quantized ANNs to SNNs, eliminating the quantization error during conversion. Therefore, our framework fully inherits the advantages of quantization-aware training". Training uses the APoT quantizer of Li et al. (ICLR 2020) with a learnable clipping threshold; refs [47] is Han et al. 2021 bin regularization (the BR track's source paper).
Assessment. This is the forward half of Contribution 1 stated as an explicit parameter mapping (scale = threshold, initial potential = θ/2, T = 2^b − 1, floor-plus-half = round), in the direction QAT quantizer to IF neuron. It does not cite QCFS, does not write the QCFS activation, and says nothing about the backward pass beyond adopting an existing QAT method.

Guo, Li, Li, Cheng, Chen, "QAC: Quantization-Aware Conversion for Mixed-Timestep Spiking Neural Networks", ICLR 2025 submission, rejected. https://openreview.net/forum?id=D4sQzdMvcG (PDF: https://openreview.net/pdf/c632e28e91b259f386f9fc22d7821fcd868acf1f.pdf)
Abstract (p. 1): "the power of the quantization bit-width in ANN activations is equivalent to the timesteps in SNNs with soft reset. This finding uncovers the intrinsic nature of SNNs, demonstrating that they act as activation quantizers". Section 4.1 (p. 4) writes the learnable-clipping QAT quantizer Q(x) = α/2^n · clip(round(x·2^n/α); 0, 2^n), Eq. (5), and then: "This is consistent with (Bu et al., 2023) approach to minimizing conversion error by using the quantization clip-floor-shift (QCFS) function to train quantized ANNs. QCFS utilize shared parameters within layers, represented as λ. For simplicity, we use the parameter α to represent the shared parameter." Theorem 1 (p. 4): "The timesteps of SNNs with soft reset are equivalent to the quantization levels of activations in ANNs. T_SNN ≃ 2^n_ANN". The proof is a comparison of the two forward equations under the assumption that the residual potential term is "sufficiently small". Section 4.2 (p. 6): "To overcome the challenge of non-differentiability in the rounding operation during backpropagation, we employ the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) (Bengio et al., 2013) to approximate the gradients", followed by gradient cases for parameterizations θ = [n, d], [n, α], [d, α], [t, α] (Uhlich et al. 2019 style); Case 4 treats "the quantization level 2^n ... as a whole parameter t, so the SNN time step T can be directly obtained through training".
Assessment. This is the closest prior statement to Contribution 1 in intent and vocabulary, and it names QCFS explicitly. Its limits: the theorem is approximate (≃, residual-term assumption), it uses 2^n levels instead of 2^n − 1 (so the mapping to a b-bit unsigned grid is off by one level), it does not claim that the QCFS gradient rule is the STE of a QAT quantizer, and it provides no independent-witness verification. QAC was rejected and has no archival venue. Its successor, MT-SNN (Guo et al., withdrawn ICLR 2026 submission; accepted by *Frontiers in Neuroscience* on 12 August 2026), https://openreview.net/forum?id=4dwAZRr9L5, repeats the claim in its abstract: "we first establish an equivalence principle between activation bit-width and time-steps: the SNN time-step T can be theoretically approximated by the activation quantization level 2^n in the source ANN." See [[#3.1.3 MT-SNN: Guo, Yao, Q. Li, Y. Li, Cheng, and Chen]] for the reconciled publication record.

You, Xu, Nie, Deng, Guo, Wang, He, "SpikeZIP-TF: Conversion is All You Need for Transformer-based SNN", ICML 2024 (PMLR 235). https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03470, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/you24b.html
Section 2 (p. 2): "SpikeZIP-TF adheres to the conversion pipeline established by prior A2S methods (Bu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2023). The process initiates with the replacement of activation functions in the ANN to ensure that only ReLUs are present. Subsequently, quantization-aware training (QAT) (Gholami et al., 2022; He & Fan, 2019) is applied to acquire a low bit-width and high-accuracy QANN. Finally, the QANN undergoes conversion to an SNN by substituting the ReLU activation(neuron) with specific spiking neuron, without accuracy degradation." Section 3.1 (p. 3), quantizer Eq. (2) Quantize(x) = s · clamp(round(x/s), α, β), then: "By setting V_thr = s, S_min = α, S_max = β, the accumulated output of ST-BIF+ is equivalence to the quantized function." Chen, Huang, Bu, Ding, Dong, Yu, "Reducing ANN-SNN Conversion Error via Residual Membrane Potential Alignment", arXiv 2608.13952, August 2026 (TNNLS submission). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13952. p. 1: "When quantization-aware activations are explicitly applied to ANNs [21], [22]" (citing Datta et al. TMLR 2025 and Fast-SNN); p. 8: "Quantized activation function in QCFS model exhibits natural compatibility with the SRMP regularization." The Yu group now calls QCFS a "quantized activation function" but does not call it QAT.
Xing et al., "SpikeLLM", ICLR 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04752. p. 2: "to express T quantization levels, a typical Integrate-and-Fire (IF) neuron requires T time steps to encode full information, while quantization only requires log2 T bit digits in one step"; "GIF neurons can be viewed as generalized quantizers". Conversion-as-quantization is treated as known background; "Unlike previous ANN-SNN conversions that rely on quantization" (conclusion).
Scale-and-Fire, "One-Timestep is Enough", arXiv 2510.23383, Oct 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23383. p. 3 lists "ANN adaptations (activation quantization (Esser et al., 2020), trainable clipping layers (Ho & Chang, 2021), and ReLU alternatives (Bu et al., 2022b ...))" as conversion tools, i.e., cites LSQ as a conversion technique alongside QCFS. Passing.
Kirin (Wang et al., arXiv 2602.08817, Feb 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08817: "the time-window length serves as an information carrier equivalent to the quantization bit-width and scales exponentially with it (T = 2^bit)". SpikeQuant (Wang, Yan, Zhou, Xu, Wong, arXiv 2510.19498, Oct 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19498: "if we take 1/(S_a · S_w) as V_th, then the fire spike count equals the integer part of the ANN output". Both are PTQ-to-spike mappings for LLMs; passing for Contribution 1.
NEXUS (arXiv 2601.21279, Jan 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21279. p. 6: "The training process follows standard Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) theory, with the key difference that our 'quantization' (spatial bit encoding) introduces zero quantization error" and "the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) is no longer a heuristic approximation but a mathematically exact identity mapping." It is the only reviewed 2026 paper that discusses the STE in a conversion setting as a matter of exactness, but the setting is bit-serial IEEE-754 gate circuits, not rate coding, so it does not touch the QCFS-QAT identity.
Sun, Ma, Pan, "Post-training quantization for efficient ANN-SNN conversion", Neural Networks 191:107832, Nov 2025. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107832. From the publisher page: "ANN-SNN Conversion constructs a quantization function to substitute the ReLU activation function in ANNs" and "We leverage the post-training quantization (PTQ) technique commonly used in quantization neural networks." Full text not accessed (paywall).
No paper identified from 2025 or 2026 (a) states the equivalence of the QCFS backward rule with the STE of a round-to-nearest fake quantizer as a proposition, (b) reports bit-identical or seed-matched training between a conversion activation and an independently implemented QAT quantizer, or (c) uses the term “activation-only QAT” for QCFS. This conclusion concerns the **backward-pass/QAT analysis**, not whether the follow-up papers matter. Their canonical method profiles are in [[#2.1.1 QCFS family and direct extensions]]: CS-QCFS learns positive channel-wise thresholds; Group-Wise Threshold Distribution Learning adds group-wise scales and codebook alignment; Error Compensation Learning uses dual thresholds; and Residual Membrane Potential Alignment regularises the converted dynamics. Activation-Aware Redistribution is canonically profiled under [[#2.1.5 Training-free conversion (AAAI 2026, March 2026)]]. None of these papers adds the missing QCFS threshold-gradient comparison or independent witness.

### 5.4 Contribution 1 consequences for the thesis

**Verdict:** Contribution 1 is partially anticipated in its forward half and intact in its verified, two-directional form.

The forward identity (QCFS activation equals a uniform unsigned fake quantizer with scale λ, L = 2^b − 1 levels, round-to-nearest, and the SNN reads it back at T = L) is not new. Fast-SNN (2023) gives the same parameter mapping including the floor-plus-half-equals-round identity, in the QAT-to-IF direction, without naming QCFS. QAC (2024) writes the QAT quantizer, says it "is consistent with" QCFS, and states the level-timestep equivalence as Theorem 1. SpikeZIP-TF (2024) proves the quantizer-to-neuron equivalence for an LSQ quantizer. The thesis cannot claim to be the first to observe that conversion is activation quantization; it must cite Fast-SNN, QAC, SpikeZIP-TF, Li/Ma/Furber 2022, and Yan et al. as prior statements, and Castagnetti 2025 and Datta 2025 as prior prose classifications of QCFS as QAT.
What remains unclaimed: (a) the statement that QCFS with its published Eq. (17) gradient rule is, term for term including the learnable threshold gradient, the STE backward of a standard QAT quantizer; (b) the exact-level correspondence (2^b − 1, not 2^b as in QAC); (c) an independently implemented witness quantizer that reproduces QCFS training bit-identically under a shared seed. No reviewed paper does (a), (b), or (c). Castagnetti 2025 asserts the STE point in one sentence without analysis; QCFS itself states the STE for the floor but never relates it to QAT.
Consequence for the framing. The novelty claim should be narrowed from "QCFS is QAT" to "a proof that QCFS is standard activation-only QAT in both forward and backward pass, with the level count, scale, rounding, and threshold gradient identified exactly, and an executable witness that certifies the identity". The "no new theory" payoff (transfer of LSQ, PACT, sensitivity metrics, ILP) is also partially pre-empted in practice: LSQ and learnable clipping have been used in conversion since 2022-2023, and learnable bit-width search has been attempted by QAC/MT-SNN. The unsupported gap the thesis can still claim is the absence of any ILP or knapsack allocation and of any Hessian-sensitivity allocation inside a QCFS-style conversion pipeline, and the absence of a certified equivalence that licenses those transfers without re-deriving convergence arguments.

## 6. Contribution 3: spike encodings and quantizer families

### 6.1 Conversion work with non-rate codes and its relation to a quantizer, 2023–2026

The field has moved, in 2025-2026, from treating spike codes as approximations of analog activations toward treating them as exact representations of a quantized activation. Seven papers are directly relevant; the rest are adjacent.

#### 6.1.1 Directly overlapping with Contribution 3

Hanyuan Zheng, Haozhen Zhang, Tianshuo Chen, Zhaogeng Liu, Yi Chang, Bin Gu, "Distribution-Aware Multi-Granularity Phase Coding: Towards Lower Conversion Error for Spike-Driven Large Language Models," ICLR 2026 (poster). OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=meDMftHUlX, official poster https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10007555, current code https://github.com/JLU-Solar/PhaseSNN, older submission-era repository https://github.com/njzhenghy/SpikingLLM. This is the closest prior work. It frames conversion error as quantizer distortion through the Bennett integral, derives the optimal point density proportional to p(x)^(1/3), states that rate and temporal coding produce uniformly spaced discrete values, and shows that phase coding with base B produces non-uniform values. It then learns multiple bases per neuron (a learned non-uniform grid) and converts LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B without weight fine-tuning at T = 6 or 8, with a 42 percent MAC plus AC energy reduction (secondary summary with formulas https://en.papernotes.org/ICLR2026/model_compression/distribution-aware_multi-granularity_phase_coding_towards_lower_conversion_error/). Its theorem is a convergence guarantee for neuron training, not a conversion theorem.

Zhanglu Yan, Jiayi Mao, Qianhui Liu, Fanfan Li, Gang Pan, Tao Luo, Bowen Zhu, Weng-Fai Wong, "Otters: An Energy-Efficient Spiking Transformer via Optical Time-to-First-Spike Encoding," ICLR 2026 (poster). arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18968, OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=oK0ISeb5Dw, poster https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10007423. Proposition 1 states an exact conversion theorem for TTFS. An Otters TTFS layer is functionally equivalent to an n-bit QNN layer with Q(a) = alpha * clip(floor(a/alpha), 0, 2^n - 1) when the window is T = 2^n - 1 steps, the decay is linear in time (O(t_k) = (T - k)/T), and the threshold decreases stepwise as alpha (T - k). The quantizer is therefore uniform, the latency is the same T = 2^n - 1 as rate coding, and the spike count drops to at most one per neuron. Energy is 1.77 to 3.04 times better than Sorbet and SpikingLM, computed with a 22 nm model that includes data movement and memory access. The follow-up Otters++ (arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2606.13016, June 2026) restates a "layer-wise functional equivalence between the Otters++ and a quantized neural network (QNN)" and adds that "the practical efficiency of TTFS is often overstated" because decoding a spike time requires a decay function evaluation, a multiplication, and memory access.

Fang, Du, Man, Jin, Zhang, Chang, Gu, "Achieve Latency-Efficient Tempora-Coding Spiking LLMs via Discretization-Aware Conversion," submitted to ICLR 2026, OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=zrGcuTNwu1 (PDF https://openreview.net/pdf?id=zrGcuTNwu1). The listing shows "Submitted to ICLR 2026" without a poster tag, and the ML Anthology ICLR 2026 index does not list it, so I treat it as not accepted. It states "a discretization-aware theoretical framework that establishes a precise correspondence between discrete TTFS-based SNNs and ANNs," claims "conversion errors are formally bounded by latency-dependent terms, drawing a direct connection to quantization error bounds," and proposes QC-A2S, which maps a post-training-quantized LLaMA to TTFS neurons. It reports that continuous-time TTFS conversion (TTFSFormer, Stanojevic et al.) needs on the order of 4096 time steps.

Yang, Liu, Yu, Yang, Wang, Wang, "NeuBridge: bridging quantized activations and spiking neurons for ANN-SNN conversion," Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering, June 2025. https://doi.org/10.1088/2634-4386/ade183, code https://github.com/Intelli-Chip-Lab/NeuBridge. Weighted temporal code q = sum_t tau^(T - t) s(t) * step with trainable tau in [1, 4]; tau = 1 recovers rate coding; binary (tau = 2) needs T = log2 N steps for N levels. The paper claims "an equivalent lossless mapping between the temporal-coded SNN and quantized ANN," embeds tau into QAT, and reports 2 to 3 time steps on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with energy below 1.3 percent of the ANN and about one quarter of a QNN (operation counting only). Note for the thesis. The paper writes the ANN side as a uniform quantizer, yet for tau not equal to 2 the set of values sum_t tau^(T - t) s_t is non-uniform, so the stated equivalence is exact only on that non-uniform set. The paper does not discuss this.

Yiwen Gu, Junchuan Gu, Haibin Shen, Kejie Huang, "Temporal Weighted Encoding: Towards Maximal-Capacity Spike Coding for ANN-SNN Conversion," ICML 2026 (poster). https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/62184, OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=ixb50TfWoM. Spikes receive exponentially decaying weights through recursive integration, "drawing an analogy to a temporal bit sequence," with temporal and threshold relaxation to fix the temporal mismatch; near-lossless conversion "with significantly fewer timesteps." The same group's precursor, "Canonic Signed Spike Coding" (v1 titled "Stepwise Weighted Spike Coding," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.17245, Aug 2024, v2 Dec 2024, html https://arxiv.org/html/2408.17245v1), converts a PyTorch 8-bit QAT ANN, uses base beta with positive and negative spikes, and states that beta = 2 gives an evenly distributed codable range while "when beta is less than 2, the distribution of A_j becomes denser at smaller values." This is the only explicit statement in the reviewed literature that a weighted code with a non-integer base yields a non-uniform grid.

Hwang and Kung, "One-Spike SNN: Single-Spike Phase Coding With Base Manipulation for ANN-to-SNN Conversion Loss Minimization," IEEE TETC, April 2024. https://doi.org/10.1109/tetc.2024.3386893, arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2403.08786. Single spike per neuron with base Q; representable values are Q^(-t) for t = 1..T, a geometric grid, which is a logarithmic quantizer in all but name. The threshold shift to (Q^(-t) + Q^(-t-1))/2 implements round-to-nearest in the log domain; small activations underflow below Q^(-T). No theorem; 0.58 percent average loss on CIFAR and ImageNet CNNs, 4.6 to 17.3 times energy improvement over the ANN.

Castagnetti, Pegatoquet, Miramond, "Trainable quantization for Speedy Spiking Neural Networks," Frontiers in Neuroscience, March 2023. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2023.1154241. Gives a closed form for the soft-reset IF as a uniform quantizer with T + 1 intervals, then proposes a non-uniform quantizer realized by a time-varying threshold V_th(t) over T steps. The follow-up "All in one timestep" (arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24637, Oct 2025) restates the uniform-quantizer view and moves to multi-level spikes.

#### 6.1.2 Adjacent and citable

Shifeng Liu, Zhijie Yang, Dongsheng Wang, and Lei P. Wang, **“VD-TTFS: Efficient TTFS Computing Architecture on Vector Devices.”** Zenodo preprint, 1 June 2026. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20482746. **Evidence depth: primary preprint and repository record checked.** VD-TTFS changes the execution algorithm rather than the representational grid: it processes spikes in arrival order and performs a sparse forward pass instead of stepping through an entire clock window. The authors report up to 73% fewer operations, 36.8× faster CUDA execution, and a measured 95.4% energy reduction on an NVIDIA Jetson platform, while preserving the original LIF result losslessly. This is important evidence that a code's nominal timestep window and its executable latency can diverge. It does not provide a decoder-to-quantizer-family theorem or mixed-`T_l` block scheduler.

Stöckl and Maass, FS-neurons, Nature Machine Intelligence 2021, https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-021-00311-4 (PDF https://igi-web.tugraz.at/PDF/252.pdf). With T(t) = h(t) = d(t) = 2^(K - t), the FS-neuron reproduces ReLU exactly on {0, ..., 2^K - 1} in K steps, with error at most alpha 2^(-K) otherwise. This is an exact conversion theorem for a binary (power-of-two weighted) code onto a uniform grid, using log2 N steps instead of N. Background for the thesis but it is the cleanest precedent.
Wang et al., "Training-Free ANN-to-SNN Conversion for High-Performance Spiking Transformers," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07710 (Aug 2025, revised Dec 2025). Multi-Basis Exponential Decay neuron generalizing FS-neurons; Theorem bounds the error by an empirical gap, a parametric gap O(1/(NT)), and a "quantization gap" ||w||_1 |alpha| tau_max /(T Delta t).
Stanojevic et al., "High-performance deep spiking neural networks with 0.3 spikes per neuron," Nature Communications, Aug 2024, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51110-5, and the earlier exact mapping https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.12522. Exact TTFS mapping for ReLU networks in continuous time. Zhao, Huang, Ding, Yu, TTFSFormer, ICML 2025, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zhao25n.html. "Large Language Models with At Most One Spike per Neuron," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05151 (Sept 2026), notes that "the first spike timing is not a continuous value" in practice.
Lu, Ding, Yu, "A Latency Coding Framework for Deep SNNs with Ultra-Low Latency," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23206 (Mar 2026). Direct training, but it states that TTFS firing times are floating point, "must be quantized" for hardware, and that with inter-layer time synchronization "the total timesteps needed for inference scale with both the number of quantized steps and the number of layers."
Matterhorn, arXiv https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.22876 (Jan 2026). Masked TTFS; reports data movement at nearly 80 percent of energy, rate coding at 10 to 30 percent spike rate versus about 5 percent for TTFS.
Kirin, arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2602.08817v1 (Feb 2026). States that quantized parameters "are then encoded into binary spikes over T = 2^bit time steps" with TTFS or rate coding, so 8-bit needs T = 256; keeps outliers as integers.
Yan et al., "Reconsidering the Energy Efficiency of SNN Inference from Analytical Perspectives," arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2409.08290v3. Pairs a rate SNN with T steps with a QNN of ceil(log2(T + 1)) bits; the SNN wins only below a 6.4 percent spike rate for T in [5, 10].
Huang et al., "Differential Coding for Training-Free ANN-to-SNN Conversion," ICML 2025, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/huang25i.html (arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2503.00301). Survey paragraph states phase coding represents 2^T values in T steps against T for rate coding, at the cost of waiting for all weighted spikes.
Zhang et al., PMSM, arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2508.14520 (Aug 2025). Polarity multi-spike mapping, T = 1, information-entropy analysis of the quantization layer, uniform signed grid.
Chen et al., "One-Timestep is Enough," arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.23383 (Oct 2025). Temporal-to-Spatial Equivalence Theory, multi-timestep IF equals single-step multi-threshold neurons.
Adaptive Fission, NeurIPS 2025. Population coding and a temporal-to-spatial memory trade; see the canonical profile and complete measurements in [[#2.1.2.1 Adaptive Fission]]. The often-quoted 1.6× memory/8× timestep trade is specifically the Calib/ResNet-20/CIFAR-100 comparison and also loses 3.21 accuracy points.
Brehove et al., "Sigma-Delta Neural Network Conversion on Loihi 2," ICONS 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3822454.3822490 (arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2505.06417v2). Graded spikes carry up to 16-bit signed integer payloads that "represent quantized activations," so the code is an integer quantizer.
NEXUS, arXiv https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21279v2 (Jan 2026). Spatial bit encoding of IEEE-754 words in one timestep, bit-exact, no quantizer.
Zhang et al., PseudoSN, AAAI 2026, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i34.40086. Section "Rate-Coding as a Quantization Process."
#### 6.1.3 Background

Zhang et al., "Efficient SNNs with Logarithmic Temporal Coding," 2018, https://arxiv.org/html/1811.04233. Despite the name, LTC retains a window of bits of the binary representation and emits a spike per 1 bit; the grid is a windowed uniform (binary) grid, and "logarithmic" refers to spike count growth.
Yashaswini, Arora, Mulleti, "A Non-Uniform Quantization Framework for Time-Encoding Machines," arXiv https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.02728 (Nov 2025). Shows that integrate-and-fire time encodings are non-uniformly distributed even for uniformly distributed amplitudes, motivating power-law non-uniform quantization of firing intervals. Signal-processing domain, no ANN conversion, but it is the only rigorous statement identified here that IF timing encodes amplitude non-uniformly.
Aitsam et al., "Benchmarking ANN-to-SNN Conversion," Living Machines 2025, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-07448-5_24. Small datasets only.
