| Hwang and Kung, One-Spike (TETC 2024) | Single-spike phase, base Q | Geometric/logarithmic `Q^(-t)` | No theorem; log-domain rounding rule | One spike; 4.6–17.3× ANN energy claim | https://doi.org/10.1109/tetc.2024.3386893 |
| Castagnetti et al. (Frontiers 2023) | Count with time-varying threshold | Uniform `T+1`; non-uniform via `V_th(t)` | Closed-form soft-reset-IF quantiser | Fixed T; non-uniform SQNR gain claimed | https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2023.1154241 |
| Stöckl and Maass, FS (NMI 2021) | Binary weighted, K steps | Uniform K-bit | Exact on `{0,…,2^K−1}` | `log2N` steps; pipeline every 2K | https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-021-00311-4 |
| Wang et al., MBE (arXiv 2025) | Multi-basis exponential decay | Learned, non-uniform | Quantisation-gap theorem | Low latency, training-free | https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07710 |
| Stanojevic et al. (Nat. Comm. 2024) | Continuous-time TTFS | Exact in continuous time | Exact mapping theorem | Latency grows with depth | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-51110-5 |
| VD-TTFS (preprint, June 2026) | TTFS execution in arrival order | Preserves source TTFS representation | Lossless execution equivalence claimed | Up to 73% fewer operations; 36.8× CUDA speedup; 95.4% Jetson energy reduction | https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20482746 |
| Kirin (arXiv 2026) | TTFS or rate | Uniform, `T=2^bit` | LLM-output equivalence claim | 8-bit needs T = 256; hybrid cuts steps 93.75% | https://arxiv.org/html/2602.08817v1 |
| Brehove et al. (ICONS 2026) | Graded sigma-delta spikes | Integer, 16-bit payload | None | Energy-delay product vs. Jetson Xavier | https://doi.org/10.1145/3822454.3822490 |
| ShiftLIF (arXiv 2026) | Multi-level power-of-two spikes | Logarithmic/power-of-two | Direct training only | Synaptic energy near binary LIF | https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01866 |
| QB-LIF (arXiv 2026) | Burst with learnable scale | Uniform, learnable scale | Direct training only | Ultra-low latency claimed | https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25688 |
### 6.3 Explicit statements of the correspondence

#### 6.3.1 Rate coding to uniform quantisation

This relationship was stated explicitly in at least four places.

| Source | Explicit statement | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Castagnetti et al. 2023 | “The Integrate and Fire (IF) with softreset neuron implements a uniform quantization scheme”; “exactly `T+1` uniform quantization intervals.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2023.1154241) | Direct rate/IF-to-uniform-quantiser statement |
| Castagnetti et al. 2025 | “A spiking neuron can actually be considered as a uniform quantizer that discretizes its input into `T+1` quantization intervals.” [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.24637) | Repeats the uniform-quantiser framing |
| Zhang et al., PseudoSNN, AAAI 2026 | “For a soft-reset IF neuron, this characteristic effectively converts the input-output relationship into a uniform quantization function”; temporal integration/firing over `T` steps is “equivalent to value quantization with `T` levels.” [AAAI](https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i34.40086) | The relationship is now routine language in heterogeneous-latency work |
| Zheng et al., ICLR 2026 | Conversion frameworks map rate or temporal coding to uniformly distributed rather than distribution-aligned discrete values. [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=meDMftHUlX) | Treats uniform allocation as the baseline to improve upon |
| Stöckl and Maass 2021 | “A rate coded spiking neuron requires `N` time steps to encode `N` different values”; FS-neurons replace this unary code with binary coding. [PDF](https://igi-web.tugraz.at/PDF/252.pdf) | Gives the representation-theoretic contrast |
#### 6.3.2 Temporal or phase coding to logarithmic quantisation

The reviewed literature contains no sentence of the form “temporal coding corresponds to logarithmic quantization.” The nearest statements are the following.

| Source | Statement | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Zheng et al. 2026 | “Conventional phase coding can realize non-uniform allocation of mapped discrete values by adjusting the base.” [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=meDMftHUlX) | A tunable phase base produces non-uniform allocation |
| Gu et al. 2024 | “When beta is less than 2, the distribution of `A_j` becomes denser at smaller values.” [HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.17245v1) | A sub-binary base creates a small-value-dense grid |
| Hwang and Kung 2024 | “The representable value range is `[Q^(-T), Q^(-1)]` with base `Q` using timestep `T`.” [HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.08786) | Geometric/logarithmic grid under base-`Q` phase coding |
| Yashaswini et al. 2025 | Even uniformly distributed amplitudes yield time encodings “far from uniform.” [HTML](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.02728v1) | Time-encoding result, not ANN-to-SNN conversion |
Note that the ICLR 2026 Otters theorem shows the opposite for TTFS with linear decay. Under a linear time-to-value map, TTFS is a uniform quantizer. A logarithmic grid arises only when the decay is exponential (Otters itself lists epsilon(t) = e^(-t) as the alternative kernel, https://openreview.net/attachment?id=oK0ISeb5Dw&name=pdf) or when spikes are weighted by a geometric base as in phase coding.

### 6.4 Conversion with non-uniform activation quantizers, 2025–2026

| Work | Grid / code | Conversion status | Scope | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zheng et al., ICLR 2026 | Learned non-uniform grid from phase coding with multiple learnable bases | Claimed and demonstrated | LLaMA | [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=meDMftHUlX) |
| Wang et al., MBE neuron | Learned decay bases | Demonstrated | ViT, RoBERTa, GPT-2 | [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07710) |
| NeuBridge | Base-`τ` weighted grid embedded in QAT | Demonstrated | Temporal code; NCE June 2025 | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/2634-4386/ade183) |
| Hwang and Kung, One-Spike | Geometric grid | Demonstrated | TETC 2024 | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/tetc.2024.3386893) |
| Castagnetti et al. | Non-uniform grid through a time-varying threshold | Conversion-style training | Frontiers 2023 | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2023.1154241) |
| ShiftLIF | Power-of-two spike levels | Direct training; no conversion claim | arXiv May 2026 | [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01866) |
| PTQ4SNN | Power-of-two scale ratios | Post-training state/weight quantisation; not an activation-grid conversion | arXiv August 2026 | [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07066) |
No 2025–2026 paper identified here trains an ANN with a logarithmic, power-of-two, or APoT activation quantizer and then converts it to a rate-coded SNN, and none states that such a conversion is impossible. The adjacent results concern FPGA weight quantization, time-encoding machines, or alternative spike codes. Li and Zeng 2022 (https://arxiv.org/html/2204.13271v2) and QB-LIF (https://arxiv.org/html/2604.25688) are relevant burst-code examples; QB-LIF characterises earlier fixed-threshold-spacing burst methods as implicitly uniform. The FS and TWE papers remain the closest number-representation results, while the Yan et al. analysis and a 2025 computational-neuroscience survey address information capacity without providing the missing conversion result.

### 6.5 Contribution 3 consequences for the thesis

#### 6.5.1 Has the encoding-to-quantizer-family correspondence already been stated or proven?

In pieces, yes; as a unified taxonomy with conversion theorems, no. The rate-to-uniform half is now a standard remark: Castagnetti 2023 and 2025, PseudoSN AAAI 2026, QAC, Zheng ICLR 2026, and Yan arXiv:2409.08290. The phase-or-weighted-code-to-non-uniform half is stated in one sentence each by Zheng et al. (ICLR 2026) and Gu et al. (2024), and is implicit in Hwang and Kung (2024). No paper organises rate, TTFS, phase, burst, and graded codes against uniform, logarithmic, learned non-uniform, and integer quantizers, and no paper asks under which quantizer a QCFS-shaped lossless-at-T theorem survives. That gap remains open, but it is narrower than it was in May 2026.

#### 6.5.2 Closest prior work, in order

Zheng et al., ICLR 2026 (conversion error as quantizer distortion, non-uniform grids from phase bases); Yan et al., Otters, ICLR 2026 (exact TTFS-to-uniform-QNN theorem with `T=2^n-1`); Gu et al., TWE, ICML 2026 (spike train as binary number); NeuBridge 2025; Castagnetti 2023; Hwang and Kung 2024; and Stöckl and Maass 2021.

#### 6.5.3 Is there a published proof or counterexample for non-uniform quantizers?

Neither: no published proof or strict counterexample is identified here. Three constructive results nevertheless determine how the claim must be phrased. Castagnetti 2023 realises a non-uniform quantizer with a constant-weight count code by letting the threshold vary over the T steps. Zheng et al. 2026 and Hwang and Kung 2024 realise non-uniform, geometric or learned grids with weighted single or multiple spikes. Otters 2026 shows that TTFS with a linear kernel is uniform, not logarithmic. The defensible statement is therefore narrower than the current hypothesis. A count-decoded IF neuron with constant threshold and reset-by-subtraction can represent only the uniform grid `{0,1/T,…,1}` times `λ`, so a QCFS-shaped identity cannot hold for a log or APoT activation under that decoder; it can hold under a time-varying threshold, geometric spike weighting, or a graded payload, each of which changes the neuron model and hardware cost. The correspondence the thesis should claim is between the decoder—count, weighted sum, or first-spike time under a given kernel—and the quantizer family, not between “temporal coding” as a label and logarithmic quantisation.

#### 6.5.4 Latency and memory relative to rate coding

The literature gives no single comparison. Weighted or phase codes reach the same level count in about `log2 N` steps—NeuBridge in two to three steps, FS-neurons with `K=log2 N`, Zheng with `T=6` or `8`—at the cost of a per-neuron multiply or shift per step and a full-window wait before the next layer can decode (Huang et al. 2025; Stöckl and Maass 2021). Linear-kernel TTFS keeps the rate-coding window `T=2^n-1` and reduces only spike count (Otters, Kirin); its decoding overhead in memory access and multiplication is now openly acknowledged by Otters++, Matterhorn, and Han and Roy's TSC as relayed by Gu et al. 2024. VD-TTFS shows that an arrival-ordered sparse implementation can avoid much of the empty-window work, reporting up to 36.8× CUDA speedup without changing the TTFS result. Continuous-time TTFS needs thousands of steps once discretised (QC-A2S citing TTFSFormer), and its latency grows with depth because layers synchronise in time (Lu, Ding, and Yu 2026). Population and multi-level alternatives trade time for memory: in the verified Adaptive Fission configuration, an eightfold step reduction uses 1.54× memory, cuts epoch energy by 71.9%, and loses 3.21 accuracy points; the complete table is in [[#2.1.2.1 Adaptive Fission]].

# Literature update, 2026-09-14

Refresh after four months away from the literature. Five research agents searched in parallel (successors and cited-by of PASCAL, QAC and MT-SNN; deployability and execution models; the QCFS equals QAT identity; encodings versus quantizer families; general 2026 state of the art and MPQ allocators). Their full reports are in [[04-Writing/2026-09-14-literature-refresh-full-reports|the full reports file]] and the synthesis in [[04-Writing/2026-09-14-literature-refresh-positioning|the positioning memo]].

Each paper below has a Markdown note in the folder where it belongs (title, authors, venue, links, summary, why it matters, relevance class). **No PDFs were downloaded**; each note's frontmatter says `pdf: not downloaded`. Download later and drop the PDF next to the note. Abstracts were not retrievable during the refresh (arXiv API rate-limited), so summaries are the agents' readings of the sources.

Relevance classes: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution, (b) adjacent and citable, (c) background. Bears on: c1 = QCFS is activation-only QAT, c2 = QCFS++ block-wise execution and the deployability gap, c3 = encodings and quantizer families.

## Structural changes

- `03-ANN-to-SNN-Conversion/03-Quant-Dist-Aware/01-Activation-Level/01-QAC/` holds only QAC and its MT-SNN continuation (PDFs, MT-SNN note, and joint status note). The sibling `02-MPQ/` groups mixed numerical and temporal precision work, including PASCAL, Adaptive Bit Allocation, LD-SNN, MTT, SSNN, SpikeMLLM, PseudoSNN, and relevant hardware follow-ups. PseudoSNN and SSNN are directly trained SNNs; MTT uses mixed timesteps in training but uniform timesteps at inference.
- New folder `02-SNN-Fundamentals/03-Spike-Encoding/` (the placeholder the MOC anticipated).
- New folder `04-Hardware/02-Neuromorphic-Platforms/02-Accelerators-and-Mapping/` for SNN accelerators, compilers and mappers, nested to avoid renumbering `03-Surveys`.
- `04-Hardware/02-Neuromorphic-Platforms/00-timestep-semantics-by-platform-2026-09.md` is a working note compiled from primary sources (Lava runtime code, Intel brief, SpiNNaker 2, BrainScaleS-2, Speck, SpikingJelly changelog), not a paper.
- Pointer notes (marked 'Pointer note, PDF elsewhere') record why an already-filed PDF matters for a contribution without moving it: Fast-SNN, SpikeZIP-TF, Datta et al., Chen Ca-LIF, Error Compensation Learning, Meyer S4D, InfoQ.

## Already in the vault, found again by the agents (no new note)

InfoQ (`07-Mixed-Precision/01-New/39039-…pdf`), Adaptive Fission (`03-Encoding-Level/10236_…pdf`), AAAI-26 Activation-Aware Redistribution (`01-Activation-Level/37148-…pdf`), Xia et al. Neurocomputing 2026 (`01-BPTT/1-s2.0-S0925231226000019-main.pdf`), Error Compensation Learning ICML 2025 (`02-Unevenness-Error/8974_…pdf`), SpikeZIP-TF (`02-Low-Latency/you24b.pdf`), LAS (`02-Neuron-Model-Level/2505.09659v1.pdf`), Scale-and-Fire (`02-Neuron-Model-Level/2510.23383v1.pdf`), Canonic Signed Spike Coding (`02-Neuron-Model-Level/2408.17245v3.pdf`), Zheng et al. phase coding ICLR 2026 (`03-Encoding-Level/9103_…pdf`), QC-A2S (`03-Encoding-Level/16048_…pdf`), Differential Coding ICML 2025 (`03-Encoding-Level/2503.00301v3.pdf`), PMSM (`03-Quant-Dist-Aware/2508.14520v1.pdf`), NeuBridge (`02-Neuron-Model-Encoding-Level/Yang_2025_…pdf`), Castagnetti 2023 (`01-Activation-Level/fnins-17-1154241.pdf`), Chen Ca-LIF 2023 (`02-Neuron-Model-Encoding-Level/fnins-17-1141701.pdf`), Fast-SNN, Datta et al. (`01-Classical-Conversion/SNN_meets_ANN.pdf`), Meyer S4D on Loihi 2 (`11-Dr-Mohamed/2409.15022v1.pdf`).

## Search audit trail

> [!info]- Internal procedural record
> This material was moved out of the reader-facing literature and positioning reports. It is retained here only so the search coverage and unresolved access problems remain auditable.
>
> **Coverage.** The refresh covered work published or materially updated from May through September 2026, plus earlier papers needed to position the three contributions. Sources included Exa full-text search and fetch, OpenAlex, arXiv HTML/PDF and search, publisher and proceedings pages, OpenReview static pages and PDFs, GitHub source and documentation, and local PDF-text extraction for about 30 Contribution 1 papers.
>
> **Access limitations.** Semantic Scholar's Graph API and the arXiv export API returned HTTP 429 during most of the session. OpenReview discussion threads were blocked by browser verification, although static forum pages and submission PDFs remained accessible. QAC and MT-SNN cited-by conclusions therefore relied on OpenAlex and full-text search rather than a complete Semantic Scholar pass.
>
> **Additional Exa pass.** A 14 September 2026 pass reviewed 346 returned results across citation status, unresolved metadata, the QCFS family, and incremental May–September 2026 work. It resolved the MT-SNN author list, Adaptive Fission Table 1, Xia et al.'s bibliographic metadata, GMPQ-TE's activation/code scope, CS-QCFS's method and authorship, and three previously uncertain author lists in `references.bib`. It did not recover the QAC/MT-SNN review discussions, a final decision for Scale-and-Fire or the separate Guo unevenness-error submission, an abstract or results for Xia et al., or new citations to QAC or MT-SNN.
>
> **Broad conversion and mixed-timestep query families.** Queries covered ANN-to-SNN conversion, ANN2SNN, low-latency conversion, layer-wise and mixed timesteps, adaptive per-layer horizons, mixed-precision activation conversion, effective or weighted timestep metrics, heterogeneous horizons, pipelined mixed-timestep execution, and Loihi/Lava activation precision.
>
> **Contribution 1 query families.** Exact and near-exact searches covered QCFS as quantization-aware training, ANN-to-SNN conversion as activation quantization, spike counts as activation quantizers, `T=2^b−1`, fake quantization and the STE, low-bit activation conversion, SpikeZIP successors, SpikeLLM, QCFS/LSQ, QCFS/PACT, and independently matched forward/backward training.
>
> **Contribution 2 query families.** Searches covered critiques of average/effective timesteps, sequential sums of per-layer horizons, block-wise or stage-wise mixed-`T` execution, spike-count re-encoding, rate boundaries, hierarchical horizon allocation, hardware pipelines, and compilers or schedulers exposing layer/block horizons.
>
> **Contribution 3 query families.** Searches covered logarithmic, power-of-two, and APoT activation quantization in conversion; non-uniform quantization and spike encoding; burst conversion; spike trains as radix/number representations; and spike-count versus spike-timing information capacity.

# Loihi latency accounting: NxTF (Rueckauer et al., ACM JETC 2022) and Davies et al. (Proc. IEEE 2021)

**Authors.** B. Rueckauer et al.; M. Davies et al.  
**Venue.** ACM JETC 2022; Proceedings of the IEEE 2021  
**Date.** 2021 to 2022  
**Links.**
- https://doi.org/10.1145/3501770
- https://doi.org/10.1109/jproc.2021.3067593

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

NxTF: total execution time per algorithmic timestep is the sum of all phases, multiplied by the number of timesteps each sample is run. Davies et al.: higher layer counts demand an increasing number of timesteps to reach maximum accuracy.

## Why it matters for the thesis

Standard Loihi accounting multiplies per-step cost by the number of steps per sample.

## Relation

- Relevance: (c) background
- Bears on: Contribution 2 (QCFS++, block-wise execution and the deployability gap)

## Flags

- Check whether either PDF is already in the vault

# Mixed-Timestep Spiking Neural Networks: A Temporal Alignment Framework for High-Efficiency Neuromorphic Computing

**Authors.** Guo, Yao, Li, Li, Cheng, Chen  
**Venue.** Frontiers in Neuroscience (Neuromorphic Engineering), accepted 2026-08-12, provisional; received 2026-01-08. Earlier version withdrawn from ICLR 2026.  
**Date.** 2026-08  
**Links.**
- https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnins.2026.1783326/full
- https://openreview.net/forum?id=4dwAZRr9L5 (withdrawn ICLR 2026 version, PDF in this folder as MT-SNN.pdf)

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Archival version of MT-SNN. Keywords on the accepted-article page are mixed-timestep SNNs, quantization aware training, scaled synaptic current accumulation (SSCA), ultra-low latency. Still reports an average of per-layer timesteps (4.88 on ImageNet) and adds SSCA, a fused temporal alignment in the synaptic-current domain that avoids a standalone alignment kernel. The ICLR version defines T-bar = sum_l T_l / L (Fig. 4), average alignment as averaging over T_l then replicating over T_{l+1} (Eq. 20, so the downstream layer receives a real-valued input whenever T_l > 1), and reports GPU wall-clock only (Table 4, 4x RTX 4090). Cites Du et al. 2025 (MTT) for stage-wise mixed timesteps; does not cite PASCAL or QAC.

## Why it matters for the thesis

The thesis text currently describes MT-SNN as withdrawn. It was withdrawn from ICLR 2026 and then accepted at Frontiers; both facts must appear. Eq. 20 is a citable statement that the mixed-T network no longer passes binary spikes across the boundary, which is the deployability defect Contribution 2 addresses. Full text not yet posted; reviewer text from OpenReview could not be fetched (challenge wall), so the reviewer objection about latency can only be cited from a saved copy.

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution
- Bears on: Contribution 2 (QCFS++, block-wise execution and the deployability gap)

- Accepted-article page verified 2026-09-14; full text pending

# NeuroFlex: Column-Exact ANN-SNN Co-Execution Accelerator with Cost-Guided Scheduling

**Authors.** V. Manjunath, P. Ramesh, G. Srinivasan  
**Venue.** arXiv 2511.05215  
**Date.** 2025-11-07  
**Links.**

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Extends PASCAL's integer-exact QCFS conversion from layers to individual output columns. Activations are stored as INT8 and spikes are generated on the fly inside the processing element (spike generation, spike count, membrane potential re-initialization), with (3L - 1) = 23 timesteps for L = 8. An offline cost model assigns columns to ANN or SNN cores with deterministic runtime. States that the effective number of timesteps is the same as in PASCAL. Uniform T.

## Why it matters for the thesis

Cites PASCAL. Its per-column INT8-to-spike and spike-to-INT8 conversion is the hardware analogue of B_count and B_reencode at column granularity, the closest hardware precedent for the boundary operators.

# One-Spike SNN: Single-Spike Phase Coding With Base Manipulation for ANN-to-SNN Conversion Loss Minimization

**Authors.** S. Hwang, J. Kung  
**Venue.** IEEE TETC, April 2024; arXiv 2403.08786  
**Date.** 2024-04  
**Links.**
- https://doi.org/10.1109/tetc.2024.3386893
- https://arxiv.org/html/2403.08786

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Single spike per neuron with base Q; representable values are Q^{-t} for t = 1..T, a geometric grid, which is a logarithmic quantizer in all but name. The threshold shift to (Q^{-t} + Q^{-t-1})/2 implements round-to-nearest in the log domain; small activations underflow below Q^{-T}. No theorem; 0.58 percent average loss on CIFAR and ImageNet CNNs; 4.6x to 17.3x energy improvement over the ANN.

## Why it matters for the thesis

The closest existing realization of a logarithmic quantizer through a spike code (Contribution 3).

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution

**Authors.** C. Stöckl, W. Maass

## Summary

With T(t) = h(t) = d(t) = 2^{K - t}, the FS-neuron reproduces ReLU exactly on {0, ..., 2^K - 1} in K steps, with error at most alpha 2^{-K} otherwise. ## Why it matters for the thesis

The cleanest precedent for an exact conversion theorem with a power-of-two weighted code onto a uniform grid in log2 N steps.

records.authors: Yan, Mao, Liu, Li, Luo, Pan, Zhu, Wong
records.content:
# Otters: An Energy-Efficient Spiking Transformer via Optical Time-to-First-Spike Encoding

**Authors.** Yan, Mao, Liu, Li, Luo, Pan, Zhu, Wong  
**Venue.** ICLR 2026 poster; arXiv 2509.18968  
**Date.** 2026-04  
**Links.**
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18968
- https://openreview.net/forum?id=oK0ISeb5Dw
- https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10007423

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Proposition 1 states an exact conversion theorem for TTFS. An Otters TTFS layer is functionally equivalent to an n-bit QNN layer with Q(a) = alpha clip(floor(a/alpha), 0, 2^n - 1) when the window is T = 2^n - 1 steps, the decay is linear in time (O(t_k) = (T - k)/T) and the threshold decreases stepwise as alpha (T - k). The quantizer is uniform, the latency is the same T = 2^n - 1 as rate coding, and the spike count drops to at most one per neuron. Energy 1.77x to 3.04x better than Sorbet and SpikingLM with a 22 nm model including data movement. Lists epsilon(t) = e^{-t} as the alternative kernel.

## Why it matters for the thesis

Shows that TTFS with a linear kernel is a uniform quantizer, not a logarithmic one. Contribution 3 must be stated as a decoder-to-quantizer-family correspondence, not an encoding-name-to-quantizer one.

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution
- Bears on: Contribution 3 (encodings and quantizer families)

Logged in [[01-Literature/2026-09-14-literature-update|the 2026-09-14 literature update]].

## Summary

Direct training with a learnable per-layer timestep T_l obtained through pseudo-quantization noise. States that the temporal integration and firing of a neuron over T timesteps is equivalent to value quantization with T levels (citing Bu et al. 2022 and Liu et al. 2025), and that a soft-reset IF neuron implements a uniform quantization function. Layers with T_l different from T_{l-1} are joined by temporal reshaping (Eq. 13), the temporal average of the previous output broadcast over T_l steps, so the downstream input is graded. Neuromorphic deployment is deferred to future work.

A fourth mixed-timestep method (after PASCAL, QAC, MT-SNN) that reports a mean of T_l as latency and has no execution model. Also a prior forward-pass statement of rate coding as uniform quantization (Contribution 1 must cite it).

# Shrinking Your TimeStep: Towards Low-Latency Neuromorphic Object Recognition with Spiking Neural Networks

**Authors.** Y. Ding, L. Zuo, M. Jing, P. He, Y. Xiao  
**Venue.** AAAI 2024; arXiv 2401.01912  
**Date.** 2024-02  
**Links.**
- https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i10.29066
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01912

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Direct-training SNN divided into n stages with shrinking timesteps T_1 > T_2 > ... > T_n. The boundary is a 'temporal transformer': the T_1-step global-average descriptor is passed through a learned softmax weighting d in R^{T_2} (W in R^{T_2 x T_1}) and the summed spikes of stage 1 are redistributed as I_{2,t} = (sum_{t'} O_{1,t'}) d_t. Reported latency is a unit-weighted mean, T_avg = sum_i n_i T_i / sum_i n_i (Eq. 10). Accuracy is insensitive to the stage partitioning (11 partitions of VGG-9 at average T = 5). DVS datasets.

## Why it matters for the thesis

The direct-training precedent for block-wise heterogeneous T with an explicit boundary operator (a learned, real-valued B_reencode). Block grouping itself is therefore not novel; Contribution 2's novelty lies in the external assignment as input, the boundary taxonomy with costs, and execution on standard substrates. Also a precedent for the averaging the thesis criticizes.

# Status note, PASCAL as of 2026-09-14 (now TMLR)

**Authors.** P. Ramesh, G. Srinivasan (IIT Madras)  
**Venue.** TMLR, published 2025-12-10; arXiv 2505.01730 v1 2025-05-03, v2 2025-12-11  
**Date.** 2025-12  
**Links.**
- https://openreview.net/forum?id=kIdB7Xp1Iv
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01730
- https://github.com/BrainSeek-Lab/PASCAL

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

PASCAL is accepted at TMLR. v2 claims a 56x timestep reduction on ResNet-34 ImageNet (v1 claimed 64x). In the TMLR text T_eff = (1/|L_tot|) sum_l r_E^l T^l (Eq. 16), where r_E^l is a per-layer energy ratio of the PASC-SNN to a vanilla SNN, so the headline 3.14 for ResNet-18 CIFAR-10 is an energy-weighted mean of per-layer T, not a latency. T_norm (Eq. 13) is the analogous energy-normalized count for uniform L. Appendix A.10.2 'Latency' measures wall-clock on the LoAS accelerator for uniform T = 4 only (0.40 s default IF vs 0.45 s PASC-IF, VGG-16 CIFAR-10); no latency is given for any mixed assignment. The text contains no occurrence of 'pipeline', 'Loihi', or 'SpikingJelly'. Theorem 3.6 proves the PASC formulation is mathematically equivalent to the QCFS ANN; Section 3.4.5 says the subnetwork is obtained 'by activation quantization'. Semantic Scholar lists 3 citations (NeuroFlex, APEX, Steennis). Acknowledgements credit Varun Manjunath for benchmarking on neuromorphic architectural simulators, which became NeuroFlex.

## Why it matters for the thesis

Cite PASCAL as TMLR 2025 with the 56x figure. The thesis critique must distinguish PASCAL's energy-weighted T_eff (defensible as an energy proxy, not a latency) from the unweighted means of QAC, MT-SNN and PseudoSNN.

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution
- Bears on: Contribution 2 (QCFS++, block-wise execution and the deployability gap)

Thesis Plan for Mixed-Timestep Deployment of QCFS-Based CNNs
records.content:
# Thesis Plan for Mixed-Timestep Deployment of QCFS-Based CNNs

The thesis investigates how existing mixed-precision assignments can be realized as converted SNNs and whether their expected efficiency benefits survive deployment. Heterogeneous activation precision determines the temporal budgets under study. Weight quantization, including joint weight–activation assignments and integer execution, is also in scope. The empirical work focuses on CNNs with ReLU-based activations, uniform unsigned activation quantization, binary rate coding, and non-leaky integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons with soft reset.

Contribution 1 establishes the precise relationship between QCFS and activation-only quantization-aware training (QAT). Contribution 2 develops and evaluates the execution of mixed temporal precision. Block grouping is the initial execution strategy. The broader correspondence between other spike decoders and quantizer families is reserved for future work.

**SpikingJelly remains the primary conversion and simulation framework.** Contribution 2 extends the same framework already used to evaluate Contribution 1 at different timesteps. Lava and the target hardware form the deployment continuation of that workflow, not a replacement research stack.

**The first priority is a validated uniform-horizon pipeline from trained QCFS CNN to target execution.** Mixed assignments, temporal boundaries, and block comparisons follow that baseline. Existing C1 simulations are the starting evidence, not a substitute for checking the conversion against an independent reference and establishing the hardware mapping.

The scope follows [[02-Notes/general/2026-09-15 Notes]], [[2026-09-14-literature-refresh-positioning]], and [[2026-09-14-literature-refresh-full-reports]]. ## 1. Research objective

The thesis retains the established term **ANN-to-SNN conversion**. Its experimental claims concern **CNNs**. Transformer and large-language-model conversion methods provide relevant comparisons, but their architectures are outside the deployment study.

> [!important] Research gap
> Mixed-timestep QCFS-based CNN conversion lacks a hardware-validated execution path that realizes heterogeneous temporal budgets and establishes their accuracy, latency, and energy trade-offs, including boundary and scheduling costs.

The central research question is

> How can an externally assigned mixed-precision CNN be converted into a binary rate-coded SNN with heterogeneous temporal budgets, using non-leaky IF neurons with soft reset, and under what weight-arithmetic and execution conditions does that configuration reduce latency, energy, or memory at comparable accuracy?

The intended progression is

**QCFS–QAT correspondence → existing activation or joint weight–activation assignment → fixed-assignment training → SpikingJelly conversion and mixed-timestep execution → target-compatible arithmetic and deployment → measured accuracy and cost.**

The experimental order starts with the uniform special case of that pipeline. Establish conversion correctness, Lava agreement, and target execution before testing whether heterogeneous horizons improve the validated baseline.

The expected savings are a hypothesis. Their realization depends on the representation crossing each boundary, the target's arithmetic, memory and communication resources, and the execution schedule.

### 2.3 Precision, horizons, and correctness

At activation site $l$, let $L_l$ be the maximum unsigned quantization index and $\lambda_l$ the activation range. There are $L_l+1$ reconstruction levels and the step size is $s_l=\lambda_l/L_l$. Distinguish activation precision $b_l^a$ from weight precision $b_l^w$. For a full unsigned activation grid,

$$
L_l=2^{b_l^a}-1.
$$

A normalized binary spike count over $T_l$ steps has the possible values $0,1/T_l,\ldots,1$. Matching its representational grid to the quantizer motivates $T_l=L_l$, subject to the conversion assumptions. An imported resolution such as $L_l=4$ denotes five levels and must not be silently relabeled as an integer-bit quantizer.

Weight precision does not have this direct timestep interpretation. It changes weight reconstruction, storage, memory traffic, and the arithmetic supported by the backend. Lower weight precision may improve execution cost, but only if the implementation exploits it. Fake-quantized weights stored and multiplied as FP32 do not demonstrate native integer execution or packed low-bit storage.

Three distinct claims must be tested separately.

| Claim | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| QCFS and the reference QAT operator have the same training behavior | Forward and surrogate-gradient analysis, parameter mapping, and matched implementation checks. |
| A converted SNN preserves the trained quantized CNN sufficiently well | Conversion assumptions, intermediate activation comparisons, and measured output accuracy at the stated horizons. |
| Mixed horizons reduce execution cost | Traces or measurements of the actual heterogeneous configuration on a stated implementation. |

The first claim does not establish the other two. Matching the representable grids also does not remove all effects of spike timing, saturation, residual membrane state, or inter-block conversion.

## 3. Literature position and contributions

### 3.1 The execution question

QCFS supplies the activation and conversion baseline [1]. The relationship between activation quantization and temporal representation has explicit precedents, including Fast-SNN [2]. PASCAL and MT-SNN provide examples of heterogeneous activation horizons [3], [4].

The distinction motivating this thesis is between assigning a temporal budget and executing that assignment. PASCAL reports heterogeneous assignments, while its accelerator timing comparison evaluates uniform $T=4$ [3]. This experiment does not establish the hardware timing benefit of the mixed assignment.

Stage grouping and temporal transforms have precedents in SSNN [5]. Hardware-oriented conversion also has precedents, including Adaptive Fission and SpikeMLLM [6], [7]. The execution question is therefore specific to the chosen CNN, quantization, neuron, interface, and target combination. It is not evidence that conversion or heterogeneous representations have never reached hardware.

### 3.4 Contribution 1

**Contribution 1 establishes the precise QCFS–activation-QAT correspondence under stated forward, rounding, clipping, parameterization, and surrogate-gradient conventions, supported by an independent executable implementation.**

The forward quantization interpretation and the exact $2^b-1$ mapping are prior art [2]. They are necessary components of the derivation, rather than independent novelty claims. The thesis must establish what its QCFS-specific backward analysis and implementation evidence add.

| Component | Existing basis | Remaining work before the final claim |
|---|---|---|
| Forward operator and level mapping | Chapter 4 and the QCFSActQ implementation | Reconcile notation and identify the exact clipping order and rounding convention used by each implementation. |
| Pre-activation gradients | Chapter 4 contains a backward comparison | Check the stated gradient regions against the actual computational graphs, including clipping endpoints. |
| Learnable-range gradients | The implementation documentation contains a threshold-gradient discussion | Reconcile the published QCFS rule, reference implementation, and witness. Derive the correspondence in a common parameterization. |
| Deterministic implementation agreement | Existing verification scripts and training comparisons | Compare the mapped range parameters explicitly, as well as shared weights. Inspect tensors and updates directly rather than relying on matching printed accuracy. |
| Training reproducibility | Existing seeded experiment infrastructure | Match initial tensors, batches, stochastic operations, optimizer state, and arithmetic settings. Report empirical agreement separately from the mathematical proof. |

Special attention is required when comparing a learnable range $\lambda$ with a learnable step size $s$. A change of parameterization changes gradients and can change optimizer updates. Equal forward functions alone do not establish equal training trajectories.

### 3.5 Contribution 2

**Contribution 2 develops an execution method for converted CNNs with externally assigned precision, specifies how heterogeneous temporal representations communicate, and establishes the resulting accuracy, latency, throughput, energy, and memory trade-offs under stated weight arithmetic.**

The initial method groups layers into blocks with common local horizons. Each block uses the fixed IF and rate-coding model. Explicit interfaces handle the transition between blocks.

Activation-only configurations isolate temporal execution. Joint weight–activation configurations test a fuller deployment setting. Using established weight quantizers broadens the evaluated configurations without turning the thesis into a new weight-quantization or allocation method.

The contribution is demonstrated through an executable method, its correctness conditions, and comparative results. The following are useful implementation ingredients but are not independent novelty claims.

- Per-layer timestep allocation.
- Grouping layers into stages or blocks.
- Spike counting, averaging, and re-encoding as primitive operations.
- Sequential and pipelined execution as general scheduling concepts.

The existing track name **QCFS++** may remain in the repository. In this plan it refers to mixed-timestep execution from an external assignment. The thesis title and contribution statement should describe the execution problem directly.

## 4. Research questions

| Question | Investigation | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|
| **RQ1. Under which conventions does QCFS match activation-only QAT in training?** | Compare the forward operator, input gradients, learnable-range gradients, and parameter updates. | Analytical correspondence and independently implemented checks. |
| **RQ2. How should different temporal horizons exchange activation information?** | Define and compare boundary representations, scaling, state handling, and any approximation. | Boundary-level reconstruction errors, end-to-end conversion accuracy, and executable interface definitions. |
| **RQ3. When does grouping improve the mixed-timestep trade-off?** | Compare whole-network, stage, residual-block, and per-layer granularities where supported. | Accuracy and cost changes attributable to grouping, interfaces, and retraining. |
| **RQ4. Do the mixed horizons save time or energy on the chosen target?** | Execute the actual assignment and schedule against matched uniform baselines. | Latency, throughput, energy, memory, and traces showing each block's activity and communication. |
| **RQ5. How does weight precision interact with temporal execution?** | Compare uniform and mixed horizons at fixed weight precision, then evaluate joint weight–activation configurations under target constraints. | Separate temporal gains, weight-storage and arithmetic gains, their interaction, and the accuracy cost of integer realization. |

The main hypothesis is that reducing temporal interfaces through grouping can retain enough of the heterogeneous assignment's accuracy advantage to offset boundary and scheduling costs. Both the accuracy benefit and the cost benefit require measurement. A smaller number of boundaries alone does not establish efficiency.

## 5. Proposed method

### 5.1 Establish the uniform pipeline before mixed precision

#### 5.1.1 Uniform conversion and deployment checks

Begin with a QCFS-trained CNN at one fixed global quantization resolution $L$. Choose and record a global inference horizon $T$, then reproduce its accuracy-versus-$T$ curve under the paper's stated conventions. $L$ defines the trained activation grid; $T$ defines the inference duration. They must remain separate configuration fields even when a comparison sets $T=L$.

The baseline route is **fixed-global-$L$ QCFS/QAT CNN → reference conversion → SpikingJelly inference at global $T$ → target-arithmetic reference → Lava CPU execution → physical target inference**. Weight quantization required by the target enters before the final numerical comparison and must be represented in both the software reference and deployed model.

| Checkpoint | Work and existing basis | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **U1. Reproduce the source model** | Reuse the existing QCFS/QCFSActQ architecture, checkpoints, preprocessing, and training configuration. Select a compatible published QCFS experiment [1]. | ANN accuracy and a complete manifest of $L$, ranges, weights, data, and versions. Distinguish an exact checkpoint reproduction from a retraining under a comparable protocol. |
| **U2. Validate uniform SpikingJelly conversion** | Compare the canonical SpikingJelly path with native/reference QCFS dynamics, not only another checkpoint passed through the same converter. | Layerwise spike, membrane, and output traces on small deterministic inputs, followed by the accuracy-versus-$T$ curve. Investigate discrepancies rather than accepting matching rounded accuracy. |
| **U3. Explain ordinary inter-layer execution** | Follow inputs through consecutive layers and residual branches at global $T$. Inspect bias/current injection, threshold scaling, initialization, readout, and sample reset. | A time-indexed trace identifying which events belong to each logical update and sample. Record where the source evaluator propagates through several layers within one loop iteration. |
| **U4. Establish the integer and Lava mapping** | Reproduce a supported exchange example [20], then map the QCFS model without changing its soft-reset IF semantics. Compare against a target-arithmetic SpikingJelly reference. | Matching mapped parameters and justified numerical tolerances. Document link delays, initialization, fill/drain, input representation, and residual-branch alignment. A generic export example alone does not pass this checkpoint. |
| **U5. Execute the uniform CNN on the target** | Run a complete uniform-horizon classifier, first with diagnostic inputs and then with the evaluation data. | Accuracy, per-sample completion, latency, memory, and available energy measurements. State host participation and all input/output costs. |

The existing `scripts/verify_qcfs_matched_snn_equiv.py` checks checkpoint staging through one shared conversion route. It is useful regression evidence, but a shared error in that converter would affect both paths. Its accuracy tolerance also does not certify bit-identical temporal traces. Extend the validation record with an independent native/reference comparison before interpreting hardware discrepancies.

SpikingJelly's sequential module calls and a target's clocked message transport need not assign the same wall-clock step to a given layer update. A consistent layer-dependent delay may be explainable, but it must be derived and included in input duration, branch alignment, and output collection. Extending a run with blank input can also change bias-driven or residual-state behavior. Do not add drain steps without specifying what every layer computes during them.

The uniform gate requires an understood and validated numerical path, followed by complete target execution. If physical access is delayed, record which checkpoints remain open. Continue the literature and mapping analysis, but do not label the end-to-end hardware pipeline complete or make the main MPQ/block study the substitute for resolving it. A faithful hardware model is the existing fallback, with its evidence category stated explicitly.

#### 5.1.2 Correct order of assignment, training, and conversion

After the uniform pipeline is established, introduce one controlled change at a time.

| Order | Operation | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Obtain an external activation or joint weight–activation policy for the selected CNN. A calibrated or pretrained model may be needed to obtain its sensitivity statistics. | Per-site $L_l$ or $b_l^a$, optional $b_l^w$, and the assignment's assumptions. |
| **2** | Choose the realization to test. Retain the per-layer policy or explicitly project it onto selected blocks. | The actual fixed resolutions used by the experiment, not only the original allocation. |
| **3** | Configure QCFS-equivalent fake quantizers at those resolutions and train or fine-tune the CNN. | A QAT model trained for the realized precision policy. |
| **4** | Freeze inference parameters, apply the declared deployment transformations, and convert to the matched IF representation. | A mapped SNN with declared local horizons, scales, arithmetic, and interfaces. |
| **5** | Validate in SpikingJelly, then through the established Lava and target route. | Accuracy and cost for the actual mixed configuration. |

QAT already simulates the chosen activation quantization during training. The main procedure is not uniform-QCFS training followed by an unrelated MPQ quantization pass. Changing resolutions after training is a separate PTQ or recalibration experiment. Likewise, converting a per-layer model and then regrouping it without checking its changed quantizers is not the default block procedure.

Use a published QCFS-compatible assignment or an existing MPQ allocator. PASCAL is the closest initial activation-assignment source [3]. InfoQ supplies a candidate for activation and joint weight–activation allocation [13]. Begin with one compatible source, then add a second allocation family after the execution path is stable. A thesis-sized study does not require reproducing every allocator in Section 3.

Record the source architecture, activation-site and weight-tensor mappings, candidate levels, clipping convention, calibration data, and allocation objective. The imported assignment must match the implemented CNN. A hand-specified assignment is useful for testing the execution mechanics but does not replace an external assignment in the main evaluation.

Train the source CNN with fixed $L_l$ values and learnable activation ranges. For joint QAT, also fix the assigned $b_l^w$ values while training the weights and any quantizer parameters allowed by the chosen method. Precision selection and fixed-assignment training remain separate stages. A joint allocator's weight choices may be retained rather than discarded. An activation-only control must obtain its policy under the declared fixed weight setting.

An allocator's ANN BitOps or memory objective need not match SNN execution cost. First evaluate its assignment unchanged where representable, then report any target-required restriction or block projection separately. Do not describe the resulting configuration as target-optimal unless an appropriate optimization and comparison establish that claim.

Reusing a PASCAL assignment does not import the correctness guarantees of its specialized PASC-IF neuron. Conversion with the standard IF model selected here must be evaluated independently.

### 5.2 Block construction

Block construction has two separate decisions. The partition determines which connected operations belong together. The precision policy assigns a resolution to each partition. Monotonicity is an additional constraint on that policy, not a definition of a block.

#### 5.2.1 What the literature means by a block

| Work | Authors | Venue / date | Actual allocation or execution unit | Guidance for this pipeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Memory-Driven Mixed Low Precision** [21] | Manuele Rusci, Alessandro Capotondi, Luca Benini | arXiv manuscript, May 2019 | Individual weight and activation tensors; a rule-based policy reduces memory-demanding tensors to meet RAM and parameter-storage limits | A direct precedent for assignment → QAT → integer conversion → measured MCU execution on STM32H7. It is not a shared-precision consecutive-layer block method. Preserve producer/consumer tensor compatibility. |
| **HAWQ** [22] | Zhen Dong, Zhewei Yao, Amir Gholami, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer | ICCV 2019 | Explicitly allows one or multiple layers or residual blocks. Appendix VII-C groups consecutive ResNet20 convolution pairs and multi-layer Inception units | A direct block-MPQ precedent. Blocks receive precision according to Hessian sensitivity, not merely their depth. The reported ResNet20 internal weight policy is nonmonotonic; activation choices must be checked separately. |
| **Progressively Decreasing Bitwidth** [23] | Tianshu Chu, Qin Luo, Jie Yang, Xiaolin Huang | arXiv, December 2019 | The three residual stages of ResNet20 or four residual stages of ResNet18 | A direct architectural-stage precedent with decreasing **weight** precision. Activations remain uniformly quantized. It motivates a candidate structural heuristic, not a proven activation/timestep schedule. |
| **HAWQ-V2** [24] | Zhen Dong, Zhewei Yao, Daiyaan Arfeen, Amir Gholami, Michael W. Mahoney, Kurt Keutzer | NeurIPS 2020 | Experiment-specific layers or modules, including backbone, feature-pyramid, and prediction-head units in RetinaNet | Sensitivity ordering and activation-aware analysis support an external allocation criterion. Monotonicity in sorted sensitivity is not monotonicity along network depth. |
| **HAWQ-V3** [25] | Zhewei Yao et al. | ICML 2021 | Layerwise integer precision with hardware-constrained allocation; residual blocks have explicitly mapped arithmetic | The INT4/INT8 operand precision does not describe the INT32 residual path or addition. Define weight, activation, accumulator, skip-buffer, and interface widths separately. Demonstrated deployment is on a T4 GPU, not an SNN target. |
| **Free Bits** [26] | Georg Rutishauser, Francesco Conti, Luca Benini | arXiv manuscript, July 2023 | Layerwise policy refined using target latency, followed by fixed-assignment QAT | Increasing some operand precisions can improve latency because kernel support matters. Results use DORY-generated code and GVSOC cycle-accurate MCU simulation. This is neither depth-monotonic allocation nor consecutive-layer grouping. |
| **SSNN** [5] | Yongqi Ding et al. | AAAI 2024 | Manually selected contiguous stages. Eight VGG convolution layers are split equally where possible, or as `(3,3,2)` and `(2,2,2,1,1)` in reported partition ablations | Supports simple, explicit stage construction and an ablation over the number of temporal interfaces. Its learned temporal transform and LIF training remain separate design choices. |
| **MTT** [14] | Kangrui Du, Yuhang Wu, Shikuang Deng, Shi Gu | ICLR 2025 | Groups of existing residual blocks. ResNet18 experiments vary the number of residual blocks per stage over $g\in\{1,2,4,8\}$ | A direct precedent for architecture-based granularity rather than inventing arbitrary graph partitions. Its independently sampled stage horizons need not be monotonic. |

These sources justify architectural grouping and deployment-aware constraints. They do not establish that every layer inside a block requires the same precision, or that a grouped activation assignment is optimal. A block used for quantization-error reconstruction, a tile within one tensor, and a group of consecutive executable layers are different objects.

Precision that changes over training epochs is also distinct from a fixed precision trend along inference depth. Neither training-time progressive quantization nor tensor-group quantization alone answers the block-construction question here.

#### 5.2.2 Monotonic precision and timestep schedules

| Evidence | Observed or imposed policy | What it supports | What it does not support |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chu et al. [23] | Prescribed stage weights such as $8\to4\to2\to1$ for ResNet18 | A simple decreasing-depth weight-precision heuristic | Decreasing activation precision, an optimality theorem, or hardware speedup for the same schedule. |
| HAWQ and HAWQ-V2 [22], [24] | Precision follows a sensitivity ranking | Sensitivity-informed assignment to declared allocation units | A ranking by physical layer index. Sorting blocks by sensitivity does not reorder the inference graph. |
| SSNN [5] | Explicit $T_1>T_2>\cdots>T_G$; examples include `(8,6,4,2)` for VGG-9 and `(8,6,4,1)` for ResNet18 | A direct decreasing-stage-timestep precedent | Exact conversion of a QCFS CNN using those horizons. Its levels are not necessarily full unsigned integer-bit grids. |
| PASCAL [3] | Table 4 includes a VGG16/ImageNet layer-resolution profile with consecutive runs of $16$, then $8$, then $4$ | A naturally decreasing, piecewise-constant profile that can motivate contiguous-run grouping | A general monotonic constraint. Other assignments are nonmonotonic, and $L=16$ denotes 17 reconstruction levels, not a 4-bit grid. |
| PseudoSNN [16] | A reported U-shaped ResNet18/CIFAR100 profile, with larger horizons near the input and output | A reason to retain unconstrained or nonmonotonic comparisons | A universal rule that deeper layers need progressively fewer timesteps. |

The literature supports decreasing schedules as a candidate, not as the default law of activation precision. A globally increasing schedule is a possible control, but the sources reviewed here do not establish it as a general prescription. An observed late-stage increase, such as PseudoSNN's U-shaped profile, is not globally increasing precision.

For the eventual study, retain the imported unconstrained policy as a reference. Compare it with a fixed decreasing-stage constraint only after the uniform route and basic mixed interface work. If tested, an increasing or U-shaped alternative must use the same selection protocol and report actual execution cost. Equal mean $T$ alone does not make two schedules cost-matched.

#### 5.2.3 Candidate partitions and assignment rules

| Granularity | Definition | Initial purpose | Precision treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whole network | All converted layers share one horizon | Mandatory uniform deployment baseline | Fixed global $L$ and a separately recorded global $T$. |
| Architectural stage | Contiguous residual blocks between spatial-resolution or channel-width transitions | First structural grouping after the uniform gate | Use a published block policy if compatible, or explicitly project the imported per-layer policy. Keep residual branches inside the stage. |
| Residual block | A complete residual unit, including its shortcut and merge | Finer granularity supported by HAWQ/MTT precedents | Make the boundary after the merge. Do not cut one branch independently without a separate alignment design. |
| Equal-resolution run | Consecutive activation sites assigned the same resolution | Preserve an imported piecewise-constant profile where the graph permits it | No precision change solely from grouping. Nevertheless, changed timing or added boundaries still require validation. |
| Individual activation site | One local activation horizon per site | Finest implemented mixed comparator | Explicitly implement every required interface and charge its cost. This is not an assumed deployment upper bound. |

The initial recommendation is architecture-defined stages, with residual-block and compatible equal-resolution-run partitions as comparisons. These partitions are chosen from the graph before their hardware outcome is known. They need not be monotonic.

| Assignment rule | Role | Required qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Retain a compatible external block assignment | Preferred when a published or reproducible allocator already supplies the chosen units | Record the unit definition and candidate precision set. |
| Retain equal-resolution runs from a layer assignment | Minimal precision-policy change | Only graph-contiguous, valid subgraphs form executable blocks. Equal precision at separated layers does not create a block. |
| Set $L_g=\max_{l\in g}L_l$ | Simple initial projection for a chosen architectural block | A proposed heuristic, not a literature guarantee. A finer grid need not contain the original grid. Train or fine-tune at the realized block resolutions and measure the grouping loss. |
| Impose $L_1\ge L_2\ge\cdots\ge L_G$ | Optional decreasing-resolution ablation motivated by SSNN and the ANN stage heuristic | State how the imported assignment is changed. This is a constraint added by the experiment, not an unchanged PASCAL policy. |

Record original and realized resolutions, block membership, actual local horizons, and the number and size of boundary tensors. Parameter count alone misses the cost of early large feature maps. Use target memory, communication, and service-time measurements to interpret partitions rather than assuming that equal numbers of layers produce equal work.

A common block horizon does not require common weight precision. Retain layerwise weight choices where supported. If the target imposes a common weight format, record that additional projection separately from the temporal grouping.

### 5.3 Temporal boundaries

Choose what a boundary represents before choosing an implementation. Let $x_t$ denote the upstream temporal tensor. Preserving its sum, preserving its mean, and preserving its exact binary event sequence are different requirements.

#### 5.3.1 Existing temporal interface contracts

| Paper / mechanism | Transformation | Quantity and output representation | Reusable element and cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SSNN**, Eqs. 7–9 [5] | $d=\mathrm{softmax}(W\,\mathrm{GAP}(x))$ and $y_j=d_j\sum_t x_t$ | Preserves the temporal sum because $\sum_jd_j=1$. Generally real-valued output currents | Stage accumulation and learned redistribution. Charge pooling, the learned transform, softmax, storage, and multiplication. It does not automatically preserve a normalized QCFS activation. |
| **MTT downsampling** [14] | Partition adjacent frames into groups $G_j$ and set $y_j=\sum_{t\in G_j}x_t$ | Preserves the total sum. Binary input may produce integer counts greater than one | Parameter-free temporal accumulation. Counts require a supported graded representation or explicit serialization; treating each count as one binary spike is incorrect. |
| **MTT upsampling** [14] | Repeat each input frame into its assigned output group | Equal replication factors preserve the temporal mean. Unequal group sizes need not do so | A deterministic resampling baseline, not an arbitrary-ratio exact rate converter. Charge repeated downstream work. |
| **Adaptive Bit Allocation**, temporal squeezing [15] | Average the source sequence, carry its threshold scale, and form the downstream synaptic input | Mean-derived current, with the paper's multibit-spike and weight-quantization conventions | A reference for joint precision and current-domain processing. Restricting it to binary events is a separate adaptation. |
| **PASCAL**, accumulation, correction, and regeneration [3] | Processes the incoming horizon, corrects residual/count error, then regenerates the outgoing sequence | A count-mediated reconstruction under PASC-IF, with additional internal corrective events | A full conversion procedure to study, not a free boundary or an unchanged standard-IF neuron. Charge all phases, not only the final emitted horizon. |
| **PseudoSNN**, Eq. 13 [16] | Identity for equal horizons; otherwise $y_j=(1/T_{\mathrm{in}})\sum_t x_t$ for each receiving step | Preserves the temporal mean. Unequal-horizon output is generally a decoded real-valued tensor | The first numerical reference for rate semantics. Charge accumulation, normalization, current generation, and reuse over the downstream horizon. |
| **MT-SNN**, current SSCA description [4] | The accepted abstract specifies Scaled Synaptic Current Accumulation, fused in the synaptic-current domain without a standalone alignment kernel | The current equation and exact normalization remain unverified from the accessible abstract | A close fused-boundary precedent that must be checked before claiming new current-domain alignment. Do not equate it automatically with the earlier manuscript's Eq. 20 mean/repeat description. |

The current Frontiers abstract changes the MT-SNN comparison. Earlier notes describing a standalone average/repeat alignment must be version-tagged until the accepted equations are available. Lack of a separate alignment kernel does not remove accumulation or scheduling costs, but it does rule out charging an implementation for a redundant kernel it does not execute.

PseudoSNN and MTT provide [author code](https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PseudoSNN) and [author code](https://github.com/brain-intelligence-lab/temporal_flexibility_in_SNN), respectively. Use these to inspect the actual interface and selected neuron path. PseudoSNN's repository also contains multispike implementations, so repository reuse must not silently change the binary-event assumption.

#### 5.3.2 A rate-preserving reference and a binary interface

For an upstream binary sequence $s_t$ with scale $\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}$, define

$$
c_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T_{\mathrm{in}}}s_t,
\qquad
\hat a_{\mathrm{in}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{in}}\frac{c_{\mathrm{in}}}{T_{\mathrm{in}}}.
$$

Use two implementations to distinguish representation from execution cost.

| Candidate | Numerical definition | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Decoded-activation or current reference** | Present $\hat a_{\mathrm{in}}$ to the receiving affine operation at each of its local steps | A PseudoSNN-style mean/replay reference with explicit scale. Receiving IF neurons can still emit binary spikes, but the boundary is not itself binary-event transport. |
| **Binary re-encoding** | Choose an explicit link scale $\lambda_{\mathrm{link}}$ and emit a $T_{\mathrm{out}}$-step binary sequence with the count specified below | A proposed interface for retaining binary transport. It can introduce additional quantization and changes temporal order. It is not automatically equivalent to mean replay. |

For the proposed binary interface, use the declared rounding convention to form

$$
c_{\mathrm{out}}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(
\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{T_{\mathrm{out}}\hat a_{\mathrm{in}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{link}}}\right),
0,T_{\mathrm{out}}\right),
\qquad
\hat a_{\mathrm{out}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{link}}\frac{c_{\mathrm{out}}}{T_{\mathrm{out}}}.
$$

This is a candidate boundary definition, not a new equivalence theorem attributed to the papers above. The link scale describes the representation entering the next synapse; it must not be confused with the threshold of the next layer's output neurons. Begin with a fixed, documented deterministic placement of the $c_{\mathrm{out}}$ events and test temporal placement separately from count reconstruction.

When the scales match, exact reconstruction of a particular value requires $T_{\mathrm{out}}c_{\mathrm{in}}/T_{\mathrm{in}}$ to be an integer. Representing every upstream count exactly requires a compatible grid. Increasing the horizon is not sufficient by itself, and decreasing it cannot preserve every value of a larger grid at the same scale. An extra boundary quantizer absent from source QAT is a separate source of conversion error. Measure it before considering boundary-aware fine-tuning.

The decoded-current reference has two possible implementations. One computes an affine operation on the averaged activation. Another accumulates weighted incoming events and then normalizes. For fixed inference weights and correctly handled bias these can be related by linearity. That does not permit moving a nonlinear neuron or quantizer across the operation. Determine whether a current can be computed once and reused, rather than charging a full convolution at every receiving step when the implementation avoids it. The resulting current state, normalization, and replay still consume resources.

#### 5.3.3 Boundary validation and cost accounting

| Interface | Operation | Role and required interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| $B_{\mathrm{count}}$ | Accumulate binary spikes and retain a count or decoded activation | A diagnostic staged implementation. Specify how the next block consumes the static value. Count transmission alone is not a complete binary-spike interface. |
| $B_{\mathrm{reencode}}$ | Encode a decoded activation into a binary sequence for the next horizon | Primary candidate for an interface that restores binary events. State its reconstruction error, event pattern, and execution cost. |
| $B_{\mathrm{align}}$ | Transform a sequence to a different temporal length | A comparison with alignment-based methods. State whether its output is binary, integer, or real-valued and where the transformation executes. |

Every boundary definition must identify

- $T_{\mathrm{in}}$, $T_{\mathrm{out}}$, tensor shape, and sample identity.
- The incoming scale, outgoing scale, and whether decoding uses a count or normalized rate.
- Rounding, clipping, saturation, and overflow behavior.
- Whether temporal order is preserved, discarded, or regenerated.
- When the output becomes available and when the receiving block may start.
- Buffer capacity, reads and writes, and host or device placement.
- State reset and initialization for the next sample.

Exact re-encoding is not automatic. With a common normalized count decoder, a three-step sequence can represent $1/3$, while a two-step sequence cannot. A boundary must either approximate that value or use a different explicitly declared interface. Existing library primitives may implement parts of these operations; their use does not establish the full mixed-horizon execution contract.

### 5.4 Correctness and state management

| Check | Required interpretation |
|---|---|
| One block at uniform $T$ | Match the ordinary QCFS SNN evaluator under identical arithmetic, initialization, and reset rules. |
| Several blocks with the same $T$ | Isolate the effect of the interfaces. A count-and-re-encode cascade may differ even when the horizons match. |
| Boundary reconstruction | Compare decoded input and output values, including saturation, zero, maximum count, and rounding ties. |
| Consecutive samples | Confirm that membrane state, counters, and buffers belong to the correct sample and are reset or retained according to the declared schedule. |
| Residual connections | Merge branches in compatible representations. Initial partitions keep each residual addition within a block. |
| Software and target arithmetic | Compare the same input samples and mapped parameters before interpreting runtime differences. |

Preserve intermediate activation and spike traces for small examples. A final accuracy value alone cannot reveal an incorrect scale, reset, or sample association.

### 5.5 Weight quantization and integer realization

Weight quantization is a planned experimental dimension, not merely a final export correction. Use an established uniform weight quantizer first. Add an external mixed-weight assignment when supported by the selected backend. Preserve the existing FP32-weight experiments as a reference for isolating activation and temporal effects.

| Design decision | Working treatment | Required check |
|---|---|---|
| Weight training | Existing PTQ or fixed-bit QAT; joint weight–activation QAT is permitted | Record which parameters are trained, their scales, signedness, and per-tensor or per-channel granularity. |
| Supported precision | Choose from the target's actual formats | Do not assume that arbitrary bit-widths are executable or faster. Report storage padding and any unpacking cost. |
| Batch normalization and bias | Fold or map them consistently with the target | Account for the resulting weight ranges and bias/current offsets. An exporter that rejects bias requires an explicit solution, not removal without validation. |
| Scale propagation | Map quantized weights, activation ranges, IF thresholds, and boundary scales together | Verify reconstructed currents and outputs against the arithmetic-matched reference. |
| State and accumulation | State signedness, widths, rounding, saturation, and overflow behavior | Use sufficiently wide reference arithmetic to identify overflow before selecting the target representation. |
| Deployment validation | Compare fake-quantized reference, target-arithmetic simulation, and exported execution | Distinguish representational agreement from bit-exact arithmetic and from native hardware acceleration. |

The C1 activation-operator correspondence remains a local statement when weights are also quantized. It does not automatically establish equality of two complete joint-QAT implementations. Any such extension requires the same weight quantizer, parameter mapping, optimizer treatment, and numerical checks on both sides. Re-proving all weight-quantization methods is not a prerequisite for C2.

### 5.6 Extending the existing SpikingJelly pipeline

The repository already has a common conversion route. `common/qcfs_snn_pipeline.py` stages QCFSActQ checkpoints into the QCFS IF model and calls the same `replace_IF_with_spikingjelly` conversion used for QCFS. `QCFS/sj_compat.py` supplies `ScaledNeuronSJ` and `eval_snn_sj`. The existing C1 evaluations at different $T$ values provide the uniform reference.

| Existing component | Reuse in C2 | Extension or safeguard |
|---|---|---|
| Shared model factory and checkpoint alignment | Preserve architecture, shared tensors, and activation-range correspondence | Store per-site activation resolutions and weight formats explicitly. Do not rebuild a heterogeneous model from the first layer's global $L$ alone. |
| `ScaledNeuronSJ` | Preserve threshold scaling, soft reset, and QCFS membrane initialization | Distinguish binary event indicators from scaled spike tensors used in software. Move scales into a documented deployment representation. |
| `eval_snn_sj` | Retain the uniform accuracy-versus-$T$ reference | Add a mixed-horizon evaluator with explicit block state and boundaries. A global loop with masked outputs is insufficient if inactive blocks still perform the work being claimed as saved. |
| SpikingJelly state management | Reset and inspect neuron state consistently | Add sample ownership, boundary buffers, completion conditions, and consecutive-sample tests. Preserve the existing half-threshold initialization without applying it twice. |
| SpikingJelly quantization and exchange components | Reuse supported operators and Lava export functions | Validate numerical compatibility and pin versions. Library blocks and export containers are not, by themselves, a mixed-horizon scheduler. |

The conversion adapter is an extension of this route. Replacing it with a generic converter would introduce another numerical path and require renewed equivalence checks. A framework upgrade, if required for a useful operator, must preserve the existing reference results before it is used for new comparisons.
