## 6. Experimental design

### 6.1 Models, data, and reproducibility

| Stage | Proposed working configuration | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Uniform pipeline validation | Existing QCFS CNN plus a small sequential diagnostic network, all at global $T$ | Reproduce conversion, inspect inter-layer dynamics, and establish Lava/target agreement before heterogeneous execution. |
| Interface development after the uniform gate | Small sequential CNN and two connected IF blocks | Inspect scaling, timing, reset, and representation transitions after the ordinary path is validated. |
| Main software study | ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 | Reuse the established training infrastructure and test realistic residual connectivity. |
| Additional architecture | VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, if resources permit | Check whether the conclusions depend on residual topology. |
| Additional dataset | CIFAR-100 after the main result is stable | Test a more demanding accuracy setting. |
| Hardware study | A CNN that fits the selected platform, with at least two different local horizons | Execute a complete classification path with all boundaries included. Use the main architecture if it fits. |

Use a fixed validation split from the training set for configuration selection. Keep the test set for the declared final comparisons. Reuse existing baseline results only where architecture, data, arithmetic, and training protocol match.

Use at least three matched training seeds for the main comparisons, and report individual results, means, and variability. Existing compatible multi-seed runs can provide a larger reference set. Where conclusions depend on small differences, increase replication before asserting an advantage.

For Contribution 1, deterministic execution tests numerical identity. For Contribution 2, paired seeds and matched training budgets help isolate the execution method. Timing and energy measurements require repeated inference runs separately from training-seed replication.

### 6.2 Baseline comparisons

| Comparison | Purpose | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| FP32 source CNN | Establish the source task accuracy | Context for quantization loss. |
| Uniform QAT and uniform converted SNN at several resolutions | Establish a competitive uniform accuracy–cost curve | The main deployment baseline on the same target. |
| Per-layer MPQ QAT model | Establish the imported assignment's accuracy | A numerical reference, not a proof that its SNN execution preserves that accuracy. |
| MPQ model evaluated with a common horizon | Test a straightforward global-run fallback | Measure its conversion error. $T=\max_l L_l$ does not automatically preserve every layer's quantizer grid. |
| Per-layer mixed-timestep SNN with explicit interfaces | Quantify the finest implemented temporal granularity | A comparator with measured costs, not an assumed accuracy upper bound. |
| Grouped mixed-timestep SNN | Test the proposed execution method | Report the actual grouping, retraining, interfaces, and schedule. |
| Uniform grouped SNN with the same interfaces | Isolate interface overhead from heterogeneous allocation | Compare with ordinary uniform execution as well as the mixed grouped model. |
| Joint weight–activation quantized CNN and its converted SNN | Evaluate a deployment-relevant quantized model | Include uniform and mixed horizons under the same weight policy. Compare against the activation-only reference separately. |
| Executable quantized CNN on an available conventional backend | Test a broader ANN-versus-SNN efficiency claim where feasible | Match task accuracy and document hardware, batch size, arithmetic, and measurement boundaries. This is not required to establish a within-target mixed-versus-uniform SNN result. |

Start the uniform grid study with $L\in\{1,3,7\}$ where compatible with the existing experiments. Preserve any additional levels supplied by the external assignment and report them explicitly.

A claim of improvement must compare configurations at a declared accuracy tolerance or show the accuracy–cost frontier. Agree and freeze that tolerance before selecting final test results. Report the observed accuracy differences even when they satisfy the tolerance.

### 6.3 Controlled comparisons

Separate the following effects rather than changing them together in one comparison.

| Effect | Comparison |
|---|---|
| Quantization | FP32 CNN against its QAT counterpart. |
| Grouping | Per-layer QAT assignment against the realized block-level QAT assignment under matched training budgets. |
| Conversion | Each QAT model against its own converted SNN at the declared horizons. |
| Temporal interface | Hold the model and horizons fixed while varying the boundary operation. |
| Granularity | Compare architectural partitions under one stated assignment-to-block rule. |
| Scheduling | Run the same model and numerical interface under each realizable schedule. |
| Hardware arithmetic | Compare floating-point software with software reproducing target arithmetic, then compare that reference with the target. |
| Weight precision | Hold the temporal assignment and interfaces fixed while changing the weight policy under matched training conditions. |
| Joint allocation | Compare separately optimized uniform and mixed configurations under the same target constraints and selection rule. Do not attribute their entire difference to timesteps alone. |

Use a staged factorial comparison rather than an unrestricted sweep.

| Weight setting | Uniform activation horizons | Mixed activation horizons | Question answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| FP32 weights | Existing numerical reference | Activation-MPQ execution reference | What changes when only temporal precision and its interfaces change? |
| One target-supported uniform low-bit weight format | Integer-compatible uniform baseline | Mixed-horizon counterpart at the same weight format | Do temporal savings survive deployable weight arithmetic? |
| Externally assigned mixed weight precision | Uniform-horizon control using the same weight policy | Joint weight–activation configuration | Do weight and temporal allocation complement each other, and does the backend exploit both? |

The first two rows establish the initial controlled study. The third is an in-scope extension, prioritized when a usable joint assignment and native backend support are available. This ordering limits implementation complexity without excluding weights from the research question. For each fixed-weight-policy comparison, report whether checkpoints are shared or retrained. Separately trained activation configurations require matched budgets and seeds rather than a claim that all weight values are identical.

Select a small set of configurations for full hardware evaluation after the software study. Include the strongest eligible uniform baseline and a mixed configuration selected by a stated validation rule. Larger software sweeps do not justify hardware claims for configurations that were never mapped.

### 6.4 Measurements

| Quantity | Report |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | Top-1 accuracy, percentage-point change, per-seed results, and uncertainty. |
| Numerical error | Boundary reconstruction error and layer or block output discrepancy against the declared reference. |
| Temporal assignment | Every $L_l$, realized $L_b$, and executed $T_b$, with block membership. |
| Weight and arithmetic assignment | Every $b_l^w$, scale granularity, stored format, executed arithmetic format, and accumulator/state width. |
| Sample latency | Time from the declared input-availability point to the corresponding final output. |
| Throughput | Completed inferences per second, with batch size, concurrency, and steady-state output interval. |
| Energy | Energy per completed inference with the measurement boundary and idle treatment stated. |
| Memory | Packed parameter storage, scale and index metadata, peak membrane and boundary-buffer storage, padding, and any replication. Report the deployed footprint, not only theoretical bit counts. |
| Communication | Counts, payload widths, event volumes, and boundary transfer time. |
| Execution overhead | Encoding, decoding, initialization, reset, synchronization, host work, and stalls. |
| Computation proxies | Synaptic events or operations, reported separately from measured time and energy. |

Mean timesteps may describe an assignment. They do not substitute for latency or energy measurements.

## 7. Deployment and execution accounting

### 7.1 Deployment route

SpikingJelly remains the primary framework for conversion, simulation, and experimental comparisons. Its documented deployment route is **SpikingJelly → Lava DL → Lava → Loihi**. Use that route as the starting point for Loihi 2 deployment, subject to validation against the selected Lava and hardware versions. The repository pins `spikingjelly==0.0.0.0.14` in `requirements-clean.txt`; that release already documents Lava exchange. The checked-out reference source and the installed experiment environment must not be assumed to be the same revision.

The existing exchange support does not make this QCFS model an automatic export. The inspected `lava_exchange` conversion path requires hard reset with `v_reset=0`, whereas `ScaledNeuronSJ` uses reset by subtraction with `v_reset=None`. Its standard synapse conversion also rejects nonzero bias [20]. These are specific adapter limitations, not evidence that all Lava or Loihi implementations lack the required operations. Resolve them through a validated target implementation while preserving the stated model. Do not substitute hard reset or discard folded biases merely to make export succeed.

| Integration checkpoint | Required result before proceeding |
|---|---|
| Standard supported export | Reproduce a small documented SpikingJelly-to-Lava example under pinned compatible versions. |
| QCFS neuron and arithmetic contract | Match soft reset, initial membrane, threshold comparison, scale propagation, bias/current handling, and integer rounding. |
| CNN graph mapping | Handle convolutions, residual additions, pooling, and readout without unsupported host work being hidden. |
| Complete uniform inference | Validate the complete global-horizon CNN and its target arithmetic before adding heterogeneous execution. |
| Heterogeneous two-block execution | Execute different local horizons, transfer the declared boundary representation, and reset correctly across samples. |
| Complete mixed inference and accounting | Export or map a complete heterogeneous CNN and measure it against the validated uniform baseline with boundary and host costs included. |

Check platform access, supported arithmetic, memory capacity, and process orchestration early. One connected global clock does not by itself prohibit different local activity windows, but those windows require an explicit mechanism and validation.

| Evidence stage | What it establishes | Required limit on the claim |
|---|---|---|
| PyTorch or SpikingJelly execution | Numerical behavior, interfaces, and software timing | Software runtime is not neuromorphic hardware latency or energy. |
| Lava execution on a CPU | Expressibility in the selected process model and software-reference agreement | A CPU ProcessModel run does not establish Loihi execution. |
| Physical Loihi execution | Behavior and cost on the actual mapped platform | Include boundary placement, host participation, and target arithmetic. |
| RTL, synthesis, and cycle-level evaluation | Behavior and estimated cost of a specified hardware implementation | Label latency as simulated and power or energy as estimated. Model the actual mixed configuration. |

Physical neuromorphic execution is the intended target. A faithful hardware model is an acceptable alternative if platform access or mapping support prevents that route. Select one target route after the early feasibility check. Implementing several unrelated hardware backends is an optional extension.

The first target probe should use a uniform horizon and consecutive input samples. Establish neuron, transport, reset, and readout behavior, then execute a complete uniform CNN. Only after that baseline should the two-block probe introduce different horizons. The heterogeneous probe must demonstrate local completion and the new interface without conflating those changes with an unvalidated ordinary conversion path.

#### 7.1.1 Preserve the neuron and graph across backends

| Mapping requirement | Check before accepting a target route |
|---|---|
| Integration and reset | Nonleaky voltage integration, no unintended synaptic-current filtering, and reset by subtraction. Disabling voltage decay alone is insufficient if the implementation retains a filtered current state. |
| Threshold and initial state | Match equality handling, one binary event per step, negative-state behavior where relevant, and the half-threshold initialization at every sample. |
| Scales and synapses | Map scaled software spikes to binary events and receiving weights explicitly. Preserve folded biases and their injection frequency. |
| Pooling and residual paths | Check average-versus-sum normalization, skip scales, graph connectivity, and effective branch delays. A supported layer name is not sufficient evidence of matching arithmetic. |
| Input and output | Preserve the established input-current or image-presentation convention and readout window. A new stochastic input encoder is a model change, not a neutral export detail. |
| Hardware implementation | Identify the actual target-executable ProcessModel or supported microcode and its run configuration. A custom CPU ProcessModel using `LoihiProtocol` does not itself run on neuromorphic cores. |

The public Lava LIF documentation describes a standard reset-to-zero implementation [27]. This does not establish the impossibility of subtractive reset on Loihi 2, but the required hardware-executable model has not been verified here. Obtain that implementation and perform scalar, layer, and residual probes before investing in a complete custom exporter. Lava's ProcessModel documentation distinguishes implementations selected for different compute resources [28].

#### 7.1.2 Research access and compatible alternatives

Prepare the Intel Neuromorphic Research Community access request during the uniform software work. Intel's published joining instructions place the principal-investigator role with a permanent employee of an established research organization. For this Master's thesis, coordinate through the supervisor and institution. The published route requires a research proposal, approval, and an institutional participation agreement before technology access [29].

| Access task | Owner and output |
|---|---|
| Confirm membership route | Supervisor or institutional PI checks whether an existing INRC project can add the student or a new project application is required. |
| Prepare the proposal | Student and supervisor describe the uniform CNN baseline, soft-reset IF requirements, mixed-timestep research question, resource needs, and intended measurements. |
| Submit and complete agreements | Authorized PI and institution use the [official research application](https://intel.az1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_9B2moVjI62gJYDc) and required agreements. No application has been submitted as part of this plan. |
| Confirm usable access | Obtain the actual software extensions, platform-specific implementation guidance, cloud allocation, and measurement conditions. Application submission is not access approval. |

Intel describes cloud access as the usual route and conditional academic hardware loans as a separate possibility [30]. Confirm current availability with the program. Do not make the thesis schedule depend on a promised board shipment or guaranteed acceptance.

| Candidate route | Verified basis | Remaining condition |
|---|---|---|
| **SpikingJelly → Lava → Loihi 2** | Documented exchange workflow and an established research-access program [20], [29], [30] | Verify the exact soft-reset neuron, integer arithmetic, complete CNN mapping, and measured uniform execution. This remains the primary route. |
| **SpikingJelly → Lynxi** | Versioned `lynxi_exchange` code implements nonleaky integration and subtractive reset for `v_reset=None`; an official tutorial demonstrates physical chip inference [31], [32] | The tutorial's example is not a verified QCFS soft-reset deployment. Transfer initial state, scales, bias, layout, and output accumulation explicitly. The automatic converter does not establish preservation of the QCFS half-threshold state. |
| **Other neuromorphic platforms** | Potential candidates if their actual neuron and compiler path meet the same contract | A paper using IF neurons or a framework importing a graph does not establish equivalence. Verify the reset, input code, state initialization, and physical execution before selecting it. |

An alternative is selected for compatibility and access, not merely because it is called neuromorphic. A different encoding or neuron model requires an explicit scope decision rather than being treated as another backend for the same experiment.

### 7.2 Latency and throughput

Measure each block's service time on the target. Logical timestep counts are insufficient because block size, synaptic work, communication, and hardware mapping affect the duration of a step.

For a sequential schedule with no overlap, a useful accounting identity is

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{seq}}=\tau_{\mathrm{I/O}}+\sum_b\tau_b+\sum_j\tau_{\mathrm{boundary},j}.
$$

Define the measurement intervals so that initialization and reset are included exactly once. If a cost is included in $\tau_b$, it must not also appear in the boundary or I/O term.

For pipelined execution, distinguish the first output latency $\ell_1$ from the steady-state interval $I$ between completed outputs. Under a constant-interval schedule, the completion time of $M$ samples is

$$
\tau_M=\ell_1+(M-1)I.
$$

This equation describes that scheduling assumption; measured completion timestamps determine whether it applies. With independent resident stages, the slowest service interval constrains throughput. Shared cores, buffers, links, resets, and boundary encoders can impose additional limits.

Report fill, drain, and stalls from the actual schedule without counting them twice. Do not identify $\max_b T_b$ with sample latency. A pipeline may improve throughput while increasing the time an individual sample spends in the system.

Compare schedules under a stated resource budget. A pipeline using additional resident cores or replicated parameters must report that resource increase. If the selected platform cannot execute a proposed pipeline, report the supported schedule and identify the pipeline analysis as a model.

### 7.3 Energy and hardware arithmetic

Charge accumulation, buffering, and communication even when a count fits in a single message. Charge binary re-encoding where it executes. Report host-device transfers and any host processing used by the final pipeline.

Fewer active steps can reduce some work while leaving other blocks, cores, or the host active. Measure idle and synchronization costs rather than inferring savings from local completion alone.

Study target-supported integer weights, thresholds, and membrane states using an arithmetic-matched SpikingJelly reference. Weight quantization can be selected for storage and execution benefits even when it is not mandatory. Compare uniform and mixed configurations under the same weight policy and overflow rules to isolate the temporal effect. Then compare joint configurations to establish the overall achievable trade-off.

Neither fewer weight bits nor fewer timesteps guarantees shorter runtime. A backend may store all weights in the same word width, perform fixed-width operations, retain idle cores, or spend the saved work on packing and communication. Report which resource actually decreases. Quantized CNN execution on an NPU is a relevant reference, but an NPU's efficient dense integer kernel does not establish the efficiency of the converted spiking implementation.

Measured energy, hardware-model estimates, and operation-count proxies are separate evidence categories. Claims about energy savings over a quantized ANN require a matched ANN baseline and a stated cross-platform comparison protocol.

---

## 8. Milestones and decision points

The sequence is dependency-based. Uniform conversion and deployment come first. Hardware-access preparation proceeds in parallel with the numerical baseline so that administrative lead time does not begin only after software development. Calendar dates depend on compute and access approval.

| Milestone | Work | Reviewable output | Completion criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M1a. Reproduce uniform conversion** | Reuse the C1 infrastructure, reproduce a global-$L$ QCFS experiment, and independently compare native/reference and SpikingJelly dynamics over global $T$. | Source-model manifest, intermediate traces, and accuracy-versus-$T$ reproduction. | Checkpoints U1–U3 pass. Shared-converter agreement alone is insufficient. |
| **M1b. Establish uniform Lava execution** | Resolve soft reset, scale, bias, fixed-point arithmetic, transport delays, residual alignment, and readout. | Complete uniform CNN in Lava CPU execution, compared with the matched SpikingJelly reference. | U4 passes without an unexplained change of neuron or encoding. |
| **M1c. Secure target access** | Prepare the research-access request with the supervisor and institution, while M1a–M1b proceed. | Application materials, submitted status when authorized, and confirmed access conditions. | Access is granted or an explicit compatible fallback is selected. Preparation or submission is not approval. |
| **M1d. Validate uniform target inference** | Execute the complete uniform CNN on the selected hardware, or the explicitly selected faithful hardware model. | End-to-end numerical and timing record, input/output boundaries, and resource measurements. | U5 passes. This is the gate before the main MPQ and block experiments. |
| **M2. Obtain and train a fixed assignment** | Import one compatible external policy. Train activation-only and a target-supported weight–activation configuration with matched uniform references. | Separate activation and weight manifests, checkpoints, and validation results. | Every precision choice is traceable and its quantizer is reproducible. |
| **M3. Validate the mixed-horizon evaluator** | Extend the canonical SpikingJelly path with staged execution, scaling, state handling, and the first binary boundary. | Executable evaluator, uniform regression checks, and intermediate traces. | One-block behavior matches the existing reference and boundary reconstruction is explained on small examples. |
| **M4. Establish the grouping and arithmetic trade-offs** | Compare uniform, per-layer, and grouped horizons, then repeat selected comparisons with quantized weights. | Controlled accuracy–cost tables and selected configurations. | The effects of grouping, conversion, boundaries, and weight arithmetic can be distinguished. |
| **M5. Evaluate the actual target execution** | Map selected uniform and mixed configurations to the chosen device or hardware model. | Complete-CNN execution traces and latency, throughput, memory, and energy results. | The measured or modeled schedule executes different local horizons and includes boundary costs. |
| **M6. Complete the thesis argument** | Integrate the proof, method, comparative results, and limitations. | Final chapters, reproducibility package, and claim-to-evidence table. | Every conclusion points to a proof, experiment, or explicitly identified limitation. |

If the first boundary loses excessive accuracy, inspect its numerical reconstruction before adding training complexity. If grouped execution loses to the uniform baseline, identify whether grouping, encoding, stalls, or resource use explains the result. Changing the partition or boundary remains within scope. Introducing a new spike code, neuron family, or allocator would be a separate research direction.

---

## 9. Deliverables and completion criteria

### 9.1 Required deliverables

| Deliverable | Contents |
|---|---|
| **D1. QCFS–QAT correspondence and uniform execution baseline** | Stated operator and gradient conventions, independently implemented checks, and the validated global-horizon route from QCFS/QAT through SpikingJelly and Lava to the selected target. |
| **D2. Fixed-assignment training record** | Activation-site and weight-tensor mappings, original and realized assignments, quantizer definitions, checkpoints, and matched baselines. |
| **D3. Mixed-timestep execution method** | Block definitions, numerical boundaries, state rules, and an executable schedule. |
| **D4. SpikingJelly evaluation** | Reproducible comparisons of quantization, grouping, conversion, boundaries, and weight arithmetic, retaining the established C1 reference. |
| **D5. Deployment evaluation** | A complete CNN on the selected target or faithful hardware model, with the heterogeneous configuration itself executed and costed. |
| **D6. Thesis and reproducibility record** | Numbered chapters, supporting data and scripts, configuration manifests, and explicit limits on every performance claim. |

The empirical contribution requires both a correct execution method and a comparison that reveals what the method achieves. A running software model alone does not complete the deployment objective.

### 9.2 Interpretation of the outcome

| Outcome | Defensible conclusion |
|---|---|
| Mixed execution improves energy or latency at comparable accuracy | State the measured improvement for the tested model, target, resource budget, and schedule. |
| Throughput improves while individual-sample latency worsens | Report the trade-off and identify the workload for which it is useful. |
| Grouping reduces interfaces but sacrifices too much accuracy | Identify the cost of replacing the original assignment with the grouped one. |
| Boundary or scheduling costs consume the predicted savings | Establish the limiting mechanism and the regime in which the mixed assignment is ineffective. |
| Quantized weights save storage but not runtime | Report the storage benefit and explain fixed-width execution, padding, or other limiting backend behavior. |
| Joint quantization improves overall cost but the temporal-only comparison does not | Attribute the gain to the observed weight/arithmetic change or interaction. Do not claim a standalone mixed-timestep benefit. |
| Only a hardware model is available | State the result as a hardware-model study and retain physical validation as a limitation. |
| Only software execution is achieved | Present the result as an execution-method study; the intended hardware-validation deliverable remains incomplete. |

A well-supported negative result about the block strategy can still answer the research question. It requires correct implementation, strong matched baselines, and an explanation of the limiting mechanism. Merely assembling familiar components or naming boundary operators does not establish a research contribution.

---

## 10. Planned thesis structure

| Part | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Chapter 1. Introduction** | Motivate efficient converted CNN execution, define the CNN scope, and state the two contributions. |
| **Chapter 2. Background and Literature Review** | Introduce only the activation/weight quantization, integer execution, and SNN concepts needed for the argument. Review the direct and adjacent building blocks in Section 3 before stating the remaining execution question. Refer broader quantization coverage to the existing survey. |
| **Chapter 3. Problem Setup and Research Questions** | Define the fixed model, assignment, representation, correctness questions, and execution measurements. |
| **Chapter 4. QCFS as Activation-Only QAT** | Present the exact correspondence and empirical checks. Proceed from theory to experiments without the superseded learned-resolution generalization. |
| **Chapter 5. Mixed-Timestep Execution Method** | Define external activation or joint assignments, block construction, boundaries, weight arithmetic, the SpikingJelly implementation, and target mapping. |
| **Chapter 6. Experimental and Deployment Evaluation** | Present controlled temporal and joint-precision comparisons, grouping and boundary studies, target execution, and measured trade-offs. |
| **Chapter 7. Conclusions and Future Work** | Answer the research questions and state the limits of the tested method. Place decoder-to-quantizer-family generalization here as future work. |
| **Appendices** | Retain the historical QCFS+/learned-resolution work, detailed derivations, supplementary configurations, and additional results. |

This is the proposed final organization. Existing drafts and code documentation must be reconciled with it as the corresponding material is revised. The former encoding contribution is not a required experimental chapter under the current scope.

---

- [ ] Compare native/reference QCFS and SpikingJelly temporal traces, initialization, reset, and accuracy-versus-$T$ behavior. Document ordinary inter-layer and residual dynamics.

- [ ] Prepare the Intel research-access application with the supervisor while the uniform software and Lava checks proceed. Record the submission and approval status explicitly.
- [ ] Complete uniform target inference and its numerical/cost checks before starting the main mixed-precision and block study.
- [ ] After the uniform gate, choose one compatible external assignment, record the activation-site and weight-tensor maps, and configure those resolutions before QAT or fine-tuning.
- [ ] Specify one boundary completely, including scales, reconstruction, sample state, buffering, and cost placement.
- [ ] Extend the existing SpikingJelly evaluator with the one-block regression case and first two-block heterogeneous case before a wider grouping study.
- [ ] Reuse the literature components selected in Section 3 and document any departure from their original numerical or execution assumptions.
- [ ] Freeze the main baselines, validation protocol, accuracy tolerance, and measurement boundaries before selecting final results.
- [ ] Reconcile the older contribution and cost-model prose with this scope during the relevant chapter revisions.

**PDF.** Not downloaded yet. Abstract not retrieved (arXiv API was rate-limited during the refresh); the summary below is from the research agent's reading of the source and was checked against the cited page where stated.

## Summary

Lava: Runtime._run sends the same num_steps to every runtime service, and LoihiPyRuntimeService.run broadcasts each Loihi phase to all ProcessModels in the sync domain and waits for DONE; run() on any process executes all connected processes for the given RunSteps. No API runs one process for T = 4 and a connected one for T = 1 in one run call. The only escape is AsyncProtocol (processes run without phase synchronization), which has documented deadlocks when mixed with the Loihi protocol (issue 314) and no Loihi 2 neurocore backend. On silicon the timestep is enforced by NoC barrier synchronization (Timcheck et al. 2026) and nxkernel exposes two schedules, fall-through and pipelined (Brehove et al. 2026; Meyer et al. 2024). Loihi 2 graded spikes carry a 32-bit integer payload (Intel brief; OSTI report), and Brehove et al. use 16-bit signed payloads for quantized activations, so on Loihi 2 B_count is a native one-timestep message and only B_reencode costs T_b timesteps. No source uses graded spikes for per-layer activation mixed precision. SpiNNaker 2: timer-tick-driven timesteps per PE (arXiv 2103.08392), a shared n_timesteps loop in EventProp (arXiv 2412.15021), strictly layer-by-layer DNN scheduling in OctopuScheduler (arXiv 2507.13736); no per-layer timestep control in py-spinnaker2 docs. BrainScaleS-2: continuous-time analog emulation with no discrete timestep; deep networks run as sequential partitions with recorded and replayed events, so a per-block duration is expressible by construction. SynSense Speck: fully asynchronous, event-driven layer processing, no timestep to set; the rate-coding T is a property of the input window. SpikingJelly (checked 2.0.0.dev1 2026-08-14, dev2 2026-08-23, rc1 2026-08-29, unreleased): multi-step mode passes one [T, N, *] tensor layer to layer (seq_to_ann_forward, MultiStepContainer); no per-layer T; the maintainer describes multi-step inference as a constant input repeated T times (issue 379).

## Why it matters for the thesis

Primary-source backing for the gap paragraph's claim that simulators and chips advance one global timestep. The claim should read: TrueNorth, Loihi, SpiNNaker and SpikingJelly advance one global timestep; BrainScaleS-2 has no discrete timestep but executes partitions sequentially, which is the block-wise model by construction; Speck has no timestep at all.

## Relation

- Relevance: (a) directly overlapping with a thesis contribution
- Bears on: Contribution 2 (QCFS++, block-wise execution and the deployability gap)

## Flags

- Working note, not a paper

## Summary

Direct training with learnable per-layer temporal length T_l plus weight and spike bit-widths under an average-T and bit budget. Mismatched T_l are handled by temporal squeezing, an averaging identical in form to MT-SNN's alignment. Section 6.1 and Appendix A.9 concede that the squeezing stage could interrupt the spike flow and lengthen latency, and answer that SpikeConverter's two-stage accumulate-and-emit pipeline (Liu et al., AAAI 2022) overlaps stages across layers so the increase is limited. This is an argument, not a measurement. Same institute as MT-SNN (Yao is an MT-SNN co-author).

## Why it matters for the thesis

The only paper found that confronts the latency objection to per-layer T, and it does so by assertion. The block-wise experiments can test that assertion directly.

records.title: Where the thesis stands after four months away
records.content:
# Where the thesis stands after four months away ## 1. Research direction and thesis positioning **Taken together, recent conversion papers point toward a broader direction: ==reducing the cost of representing and propagating activations while retaining accuracy.**== Error Compensation Learning targets accurate conversion with very few timesteps; Differential Coding reduces spike traffic by transmitting changes in activation information rather than repeatedly representing the rate. [Liu et al., ICML 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/liu25bl.html); [Huang et al., ICML 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/huang25i.html). ==**Low timesteps, quantization, and mixed precision are closely connected branches of that direction.**== PASCAL makes this connection explicit by assigning different QCFS quantization resolutions to different layers and mapping those resolutions to their timestep budgets. [Ramesh and Srinivasan, PASCAL, §§3.4 and 4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01730v2). **Recent ANN-to-SNN conversion research treats activation representation and precision as major determinants of efficiency. Heterogeneous temporal budgets are an established branch alongside richer spike encodings, training-free conversion, and hardware-aware representation design.** PASCAL, QAC, and MT-SNN provide direct mixed-horizon conversion examples; ==Adaptive Bit Allocation and PseudoSNN show related developments in directly trained SNNs==. Differential Coding illustrates the alternative-encoding branch, while Adaptive Fission explicitly designs a representation around neuromorphic hardware constraints. [PASCAL](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01730v2); [QAC](https://openreview.net/forum?id=D4sQzdMvcG); [Differential Coding](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/huang25i.html); [Adaptive Fission](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/e2e0a9004132490db1be58bffa419268-Abstract-Conference.html). **This thesis takes the heterogeneous-temporal-budget branch.** Contribution 2 uses existing assignments and investigates their executable realization in converted CNNs. Its ==novelty must come from the execution method and the accuracy, energy, latency, throughput, and boundary-cost trade-offs it establishes==—not from inventing mixed precision, discovering block grouping, or being the first conversion work to consider hardware. ### 1.1 How the field's direction connects to the thesis The thesis retains the established term **ANN-to-SNN conversion**. Its empirical and deployment work focuses on **convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with ReLU-based activations**. Transformer architectures are outside the experimental scope. Their conversion methods inform the related-work discussion where relevant to quantization, temporal precision, or execution. | Direction | Meaning in the literature | Connection to the thesis | |---|---|---| | **Preserve accuracy with fewer timesteps** | A broad objective across ANN-to-SNN conversion: reduce the temporal work needed to represent and propagate activations | The shared motivation. The thesis must evaluate against competitive uniform low-`T` conversion as well as mixed-`T` methods | | **Treat conversion explicitly through quantization** | Quantized activations and spiking representations are analysed together; QAT and conversion increasingly share methods and vocabulary | **Contribution 1** establishes the precise QCFS–activation-QAT identity, including the backward rule and executable witness. It makes the connection rigorous within QCFS; it does not claim to originate the field's quantization interpretation | | **Give different layers different temporal budgets** | Per-layer quantization resolution and timestep allocation replace a single network-wide budget in an active branch of the literature | Supplies existing MPQ/PASCAL assignments as inputs. **Contribution 2** investigates how those heterogeneous budgets translate into execution on neuromorphic platforms and whether their expected savings survive deployment | ### 1.2 Recent works establishing the direction The table starts with QCFS (ICLR 2022), the foundational conversion method for this thesis, followed by the 2025–2026 developments and explicitly labelled direct-training evidence. The methods support the direction of research; their execution evidence determines how far each has connected the algorithm to hardware. This resembles the **research direction** explored in the original QCFS+ and QCFS++ attempts—learning a global resolution, then per-layer resolutions—although its training mechanism is different. Its relevance is that learning temporal precision is an active research problem already being pursued by others. The decision to leave allocator design behind therefore remains well motivated. The thesis can take assignments from the existing MPQ literature or PASCAL and concentrate on **connecting these algorithmic contributions to execution on neuromorphic platforms**. PseudoSNN's deferred neuromorphic validation illustrates why this is a substantive next question. The history and current scope are recorded in [[00-CONTRIBUTIONS]]. ### 1.5 The deployment question that motivates Contribution 2 **The objective is to connect algorithmic advances in ANN-to-SNN conversion to neuromorphic deployment, so that converted CNNs can realize—and demonstrate—the expected energy savings of sparse spiking computation.** Those savings are the motivation to test, rather than an assumption guaranteed by conversion. An allocator can identify a configuration in which some layers use fewer representational levels while maintaining the target accuracy. A software evaluator can establish that the resulting converted model retains accuracy under its chosen temporal semantics. Neither automatically establishes that a hardware implementation spends fewer cycles or less energy on those layers, or that the savings survive communication with the next layer. PASCAL provides a concrete example. Its heterogeneous assignments demonstrate an algorithmic accuracy–budget trade-off, while its accelerator timing experiment evaluates a separate uniform-`T=4` configuration. **The uniform experiment does not validate the execution benefit of the mixed assignment.** The connection between that assignment and accelerator execution remains to be demonstrated. Its energy-weighted `T_eff` is a proxy, not a measured duration. [PASCAL, §4.3 and Appendix A.10](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01730v2) The question is specific to realizing the heterogeneous activation budgets under study, not to whether conversion has ever reached hardware. In addition to [Quartz on Loihi](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.16795v2) and [Sigma-Delta conversion on Loihi 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.06417v2), **Adaptive Fission, NSLLM, and SpikeMLLM are close precedents**, mapped in Section 1.3. Adaptive Fission evaluates hardware-friendly precision allocation on physical Lynxi hardware, including converted models. NSLLM connects mixed binary-spike representations with FPGA deployment, although its precise deployed profile and boundary schedule still need supplement-level confirmation. SpikeMLLM includes RTL synthesis and cycle-level evaluation of its asymmetric temporal design. [Adaptive Fission, §6.2](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/e2e0a9004132490db1be58bffa419268-Paper-Conference.pdf); [NSLLM](https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwaf551); [SpikeMLLM, §4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.18610v1#S4.SS3). **The proposed contribution is an execution method for externally assigned activation precision in QCFS-based CNNs, together with the trade-offs it establishes.** It is not a claim to be first at mixed precision, block grouping, or conversion-to-hardware integration. Whether block-wise realization is useful remains an experimental question. Physical neuromorphic hardware is the intended deployment target. **A credible hardware model is also meaningful evidence:** RTL implementation, synthesis, and cycle-accurate evaluation can test the actual mixed-horizon schedule before silicon is available. Such an evaluation must model the heterogeneous configuration itself, including boundaries, buffering, synchronization, and resource constraints, and distinguish simulated latency and estimated energy from physical measurements. Uniform-horizon hardware results or software accuracy alone cannot substitute for that test. ### 1.6 Thesis progression and the role of blocks | Step | Role in the thesis | Intended outcome | |---|---|---| | **Contribution 1: establish the precise quantization interpretation** | Identify QCFS with activation-only QAT under the stated forward and backward conventions | A rigorous basis for bringing established quantization methods into the QCFS pipeline | | **Use existing allocation methods** | Import an activation-MPQ assignment from PASCAL or the wider MPQ literature | A concrete heterogeneous precision/budget configuration; allocator design is outside the current contribution | | **Contribution 2: realize and evaluate the assignment** | Develop an executable conversion path for the chosen neuromorphic substrate or faithful hardware model | Determine whether the predicted advantages survive conversion, representation changes, scheduling, and communication | | **Start with block-wise execution** | Group layers into timestep-homogeneous blocks and make the inter-block interfaces explicit | Test whether fewer temporal interfaces retain enough allocation benefit to improve the accuracy–energy–latency trade-off | **Blocks are a starting hypothesis, not a claim to the best or ultimate architecture.** Their appeal is that ordinary execution can be retained inside each block while heterogeneous horizons are handled at fewer explicit interfaces. Their usefulness must be established against competitive uniform-`T` and per-layer alternatives. Boundary costs may outweigh savings, and improvements in energy, single-sample latency, and steady-state throughput must be distinguished. The thesis progression is therefore: **establish the quantization interpretation → use existing allocation methods → investigate whether their predicted advantages survive executable conversion on neuromorphic platforms.** The recent literature supports the relevance of that question; the experiments will determine whether block-wise execution is an effective answer. --- ## 2. Scale-and-Fire uses multiple thresholds | Motivation, not a threat. They widen the per-step channel and still require a stated execution model. The thesis must define its target as binary, at most one spike per neuron per step, with reset by subtraction | | Uniform-`T` QCFS on CNNs | The QCFS group's August 2026 paper still calls QCFS the state-of-the-art baseline; Error Compensation Learning reports 94.75 on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 at `T=2` | The uniform baseline remains relevant and must anchor the comparison | | External assignment source | InfoQ supplies per-layer activation sensitivity scores and an ILP; PASCAL supplies the closest QCFS-specific heuristic; MetaMix is the activation-only MPQ precedent | Use one or more as inputs, but do not turn allocator design into the contribution | | SNN-internal MPQ | PTQ4SNN is the principal 2026 SNN-internal mixed-precision allocator in this review | Cite as adjacent allocation work, not as a block-execution solution | --- ## 5. Contribution 1, the identity **Verdict: the forward half is anticipated; the verified two-directional form is intact.** Prior statements, in order of strength, all of which Chapter 4 must cite before its own claim: - Fast-SNN (Hu et al., TPAMI 2023, in the vault). Section 3.1 states the mapping verbatim, μ = θ/2, T = 2^b − 1, θ = s, floor(x + 0.5) = round(x), in the QAT-to-IF direction, without naming QCFS, and says the framework "fully inherits the advantages of quantization-aware training". Backward pass not analyzed (inherits APoT). - QAC (OpenReview). Writes the learnable-clipping QAT quantizer, says it "is consistent with" QCFS, and states Theorem 1, T ≃ 2^n, under a small-residual assumption. Uses 2^n levels, not 2^n − 1. Uses the STE for its own quantizer; no claim about QCFS's gradient. MT-SNN and PseudoSNN restate it. - SpikeZIP-TF (You et al., ICML 2024, in the vault). Lemma A3.1 proves the LSQ-quantizer-to-ST-BIF equivalence at equilibrium with V_thr = s. Places QCFS in the "QAT then convert" pipeline; does not analyze it. - Li, Ma, Furber (Frontiers 2022). "Applying a fake quantization to ANN activation", activation-only, with LSQ. QCFS cited as related work only. - Castagnetti et al. 2023 (in the vault) and 2025. IF soft reset as a uniform quantizer with T + 1 intervals; the 2025 paper says in one sentence that QCFS is trained with SGD and a straight-through estimator for the quantized activation. - Datta et al. (TMLR 2025, in the vault as SNN_meets_ANN.pdf), Chen et al. Ca-LIF (Frontiers 2023, in the vault), Yan et al. (arXiv 2409.08290, QNN-SNN twin theorem, ⌈log2(T + 1)⌉ bits), and passing remarks in QCFS itself (STE for the floor), Free Lunch 2021, SpikeLLM, Kirin, SpikeQuant, NEXUS. What no paper does: (a) show that QCFS's published gradient rule, including the learnable threshold gradient, is term for term the STE backward of a standard QAT quantizer; (b) get the level count exactly right (2^b − 1, not 2^b); (c) reproduce QCFS training bit-identically with an independently implemented witness quantizer under a shared seed. Those three are the contribution. The chapter's opening and the abstract of the equivalence paper should be narrowed from "QCFS is QAT" to "a proof that QCFS is standard activation-only QAT in forward and backward pass, with level count, scale, rounding and threshold gradient identified exactly, certified by an executable witness". The "no new theory" payoff is also partly pre-empted in practice: LSQ and learnable clipping have been used in conversion since 2022 to 2023, and learnable bit-width search was attempted by QAC and MT-SNN. The transfer the thesis can still claim as unoccupied is ILP or knapsack allocation and Hessian-sensitivity allocation inside a QCFS-style pipeline. SpikeLLM's Optimal Brain Spiking is the only reviewed Hessian-based analogue, and it allocates LLM spike steps rather than training a converted network. --- ## 6. Contribution 3, encodings and quantizer families **Stated in pieces, never as a taxonomy; and the hypothesis needs one correction.** - Rate coding as uniform quantization is now a standard remark (Castagnetti 2023 and 2025, PseudoSNN 2026, Zheng et al. ICLR 2026, Stöckl and Maass 2021). Not claimable as new. - The non-uniform half exists in fragments. Zheng et al. (ICLR 2026, in the vault) frame conversion error as quantizer distortion (Bennett integral) and say phase coding with base B gives non-uniform values, then learn multiple bases; Gu et al. (CSS 2024, in the vault) say a base below 2 densifies small values; Hwang and Kung (TETC 2024) realize a geometric grid Q^{−t} with a single spike, a log quantizer in all but name. Nobody organizes rate, TTFS, phase, burst and graded codes against uniform, log, learned and integer grids, and nobody asks under which quantizer a QCFS-shaped lossless-at-T theorem survives. - **Correction.** Otters (ICLR 2026) proves that TTFS with a *linear* kernel and stepwise threshold is exactly an n-bit *uniform* quantizer with T = 2^n − 1, the same window as rate coding. A logarithmic grid comes from the decoder (exponential kernel, geometric spike weighting, time-varying threshold as in Castagnetti 2023, or a graded payload), not from "temporal coding" as a label. Contribution 3 should be stated as decoder-to-quantizer-family, not encoding-name-to-quantizer-family. - "Conversion does not hold under a non-uniform quantizer" has neither a proof nor a counterexample in print. The defensible statement: a count decoder with constant threshold and reset by subtraction reaches only the uniform grid {0, 1/T, ..., 1}·λ, so a QCFS-shaped identity cannot hold for a log or APoT activation under that decoder; it can hold under a changed neuron model, at a hardware cost that must be stated. - The reviewed literature contains neither an ANN trained with a log, power-of-two, or APoT activation quantizer and then converted to a rate-coded SNN, nor a statement that such a conversion is impossible. - Overhead question: weighted and phase codes reach N levels in about log2 N steps at the cost of a per-step multiply or shift and a full-window wait before the next layer decodes; linear TTFS keeps the rate window and only cuts spike count; TTFS decoding overhead is now openly conceded (Otters++, Matterhorn); discretized continuous-time TTFS needs thousands of steps (QC-A2S citing TTFSFormer) and its latency grows with depth under layer synchronization (Lu, Ding, Yu 2026). --- ## 7. Concrete edits to the thesis, in order 1. `02-background.tex`, Section 2.6, gap paragraph: MT-SNN status (withdrawn from ICLR 2026, accepted Frontiers 2026); PASCAL as TMLR with energy-weighted T_eff; add PseudoSNN and Adaptive Bit Allocation as the fourth and fifth mixed-T methods; add LD-SNN and SSNN as precursors; rewrite the platform sentence (Loihi, TrueNorth, SpiNNaker, SpikingJelly global timestep; BrainScaleS-2 sequential partitions; Speck asynchronous); cite Intel's runtime model and ELSA for the two execution models. 2. `02-background.tex`, Section 2.4.3 or the mixed-timesteps paragraph: cite SpikingJelly 2.0 count and bin layers. 3. `02-background.tex`, uniform-grid gap paragraph: replace "no published result pairs the two" with the narrower claim (fragments exist in Zheng 2026, Gu 2024, Hwang and Kung 2024, Castagnetti 2023; no taxonomy, no theorem question). 4. `02-background.tex`, low-latency section: add Chen et al. 2026 (QCFS group), PMSM, Scale-and-Fire, CKA distillation, AAAI-26 training-free, and a sentence fixing the thesis's spike model. 5. `04-equivalence.tex`, opening: add the prior-statement paragraph (Fast-SNN, QAC, SpikeZIP-TF, Li/Ma/Furber, Castagnetti, Datta, Yan) and narrow the claim to backward pass, exact level count, and witness. 6. `03-problem-setup.tex`, Contribution 2: name SSNN and MTT as block-grouping precedents; state the Loihi 2 graded-spike consequence for B_count; add the PASC-IF serial latency from APEX to the worked example if useful. 7. `03-problem-setup.tex`, Contribution 3: restate as decoder-to-quantizer-family. 8. `references.bib`: update `ramesh2025pascal` (TMLR) and `guo2026mtsnn` (Frontiers); add the entries listed in the literature update.
